items.title: A statewide mystery caller study of real-world availability of contraception in Connecticut pharmacies.
items.abstract: There is limited knowledge regarding availability of over-the-counter emergency contraceptive pill (OTC EC), ulipristal acetate emergency contraceptive pill (UPA EC), and over-the-counter progestin-only oral contraceptive pills (OTC POP) in Connecticut's supportive legislative environment. This study evaluated real-world availability of these products in Connecticut pharmacies. We conducted a statewide mystery-caller study of 532 pharmacies between June and August 2025. Each pharmacy was contacted twice, posing once as an adult and once as a minor, using a standardized script to assess product availability and location. Pharmacies were randomized to caller sequence (i.e., whether the first call was conducted as an adult or minor). Chi-square tests assessed differences by caller identity, call sequence effects (i.e., whether the initial call prompted stocking), pharmacy type, and geographic location. Overall, 7.7% of pharmacies consistently stocked all three contraceptive methods across both calls. Consistent availability was highest for OTC EC (74.4%), followed by OTC POP (48.3%) and UPA EC (13.2%). Availability was similar by caller type, except for OTC EC, which was more frequently reported as available to adult callers than minor callers (83.3% vs 78.4%, p=0.043). Consistent availability varied by county (p=0.016) and pharmacy type (p<0.001), with retail pharmacies more likely to consistently stock all methods than supermarket, hospital, and independent pharmacies. Consistent unlocked aisle placement was reported by 7.6% of pharmacies for OTC EC and 13.2% for OTC POP. Despite supportive state policies, pharmacy-based access to ECs and OTC POP remains limited and geographically variable. Strengthening pharmacy-level support is critical to ensuring reliable and equitable contraceptive access.

items.title: Long-term exposures to low concentrations of fine particles (PM 2.5 ) from vehicular exhausts and residential wood combustion and the incidence of dementia and Alzheimer's disease.
items.abstract: Long-term exposure to fine particulate matter (PM2.5; aerodynamic diameter ≤ 2.5μm) has been associated with dementia and Alzheimer's disease (AD). However, little is known about whether low levels of source-specific PM2.5 are associated with cognitive decline. We investigated associations between long-term exposure to low concentrations of PM2.5 from key local sources, i.e., vehicular exhausts and residential wood combustion, and dementia and AD incidence. We followed adults from Helsinki and Vantaa, Finland, who participated in the FINRISK population surveys in 1992, 1997, 2002, 2007, or 2012, until 2022 using register data. Modelled outdoor PM2.5 concentrations (3- to 15-year averages) were linked to participants' residential addresses. We used Cox proportional hazards models and adjusted for potential confounders. Of the participants (N = 5487), 601 developed dementia and 500 developed AD during the follow-up. The annual mean outdoor concentrations (standard deviations) of PM2.5 from vehicular exhausts and residential wood combustion were 1.06 μg/m3 (0.95) and 0.45 μg/m3 (0.21), respectively. We found no association between PM2.5 from vehicular exhausts or from residential wood combustion and dementia incidence. The hazard ratios (HRs) for a 0.1 μg/m3 increase in PM2.5 were 0.95 (95% CI: 0.85, 1.05) and 1.23 (95% CI: 0.79, 1.92), respectively. However, HRs for the latter were consistently elevated in different models. No associations were observed for AD. Exposure to PM2.5 from vehicular exhausts or residential wood combustion was not associated with dementia or AD in this study. Air pollution levels may have been too low to cause significant health effects.

items.title: Early COVID-19 Public Health Emergency Disruption and Non-COVID Infection-Related Hospitalizations in Home Health Care.
items.abstract: Using linked national Medicare data from 2019-2020, we examined non-COVID infection-related hospitalizations across 7,956,006 home health care (HHC) episodes before and immediately after COVID-19 public health emergency onset. In adjusted models, the early public health emergency (PHE) period was not associated with hospitalization among White patients; Black patients experienced a significant increase, narrowing the pre-PHE Black-White difference. Findings highlight the need for resilient HHC infection monitoring and escalation pathways during public health disruptions.

items.title: Public Health Nurse-Led Infection Control in an Evacuation Center: Lessons from the Eaton Wildfire Response Case Report.
items.abstract: In January 2025, infection control strategies were implemented at an Eaton wildfire evacuation center. Standardized risk assessments, symptom screenings, and surveillance processes were implemented. Systematic daily monitoring of symptoms enabled early identification of respiratory illness (27.9%) and gastrointestinal (GI) illness symptoms (12.4%). This informed real-time decisions on isolation areas, staffing, and sanitation protocols. Despite resource-limited surveillance approaches, implementing public health nursing expertise can effectively support rapid decision-making and health prevention in disaster settings.

items.title: A Digital Ultrasonic Height Measurement Device for Children Aged Under Five Years show high reliability yet variable accuracy.
items.abstract: Accurate height measurement is essential for monitoring child growth. Our aim was to assess the reliability and accuracy of a handheld ultrasonic measurement device compared with a standard measurement board METHODS: We used a cross-sectional methods-comparison study design with experts measuring n=57 children aged 0-5 years in metropolitan Melbourne, Australia. The ultrasonic device was our index test and the measurement board, our reference test. The ultrasonic device demonstrated a similar reliability to the board with a technical error of measurement (TEM) of 0.25cm (95%CI: 0.22, 0.28cm) and 0.19cm (95%CI: 0.17, 0.22) respectively, both within current standards. F-test ratios (ultrasonic vs. board) for intra-measurer TEMs were higher for children ≤2 years at 1.39 (95% CI: 1.03, 1.87; p=0.03) than children >2 years at 1.20 (95%CI: 0.94, 1.51; p=0.14). The ultrasonic device measured children slightly taller than the board (mean difference 0.20 cm; 95% CI: 0.02, 0.38; SD=0.67; p<0.01), with a larger difference in older children who were measured standing (0.35 cm; p=0.01). The Bland Altman 95% limits of agreement ranged from -1.13cm to 1.53cm, demonstrating variance in the measurements between the different tools. We found that the ultrasonic device showed high reliability for children under 5 years when compared to the board, though accuracy was variable, with greater bias found in older children. Further testing is required to identify the source of inaccuracies and also evaluate reliability in other contexts.

items.title: US legal definitions of ultra-processed food depart from the research construct in different ways.
items.abstract: Definitions of ultra-processed food (UPF) are multiplying in US law and policy. California enacted a statutory definition in 2025, two Senate bills introduced in 2026 propose federal labeling triggers, and in August 2026 a white paper proposing a federal definition was submitted for interagency review. The white paper is a non-binding notice, and its text has not been released. It is nonetheless likely to become a reference point for states, retailers and researchers. Most evidence on UPF and health comes from studies in which trained coders assigned foods to Nova group 4 and exposure was expressed as the dietary share of those foods. A legal definition must instead classify individual products from ingredient lists, without case-by-case expert judgment. This Perspective proposes three tests for that translation. Construct preservation asks whether the legal rule selects the same products as the research classification. Dimensional consistency asks whether products leave the regulated category on the same basis on which they enter it. Evaluability asks whether changes in regulatory status can be read as changes in the exposure that the evidence links to health outcomes. The tests are applied to the two definitions that are fully specified in the public record. The operational definition recommended by the Healthy Eating Research expert panel appears to track Nova at the level of the food supply but lacks product-level validation, and its nutrient-based exemption fails the dimensional consistency test. California's definition satisfies dimensional consistency by design but defines a narrower category than the one examined in most UPF research. The tests do not presuppose any position on Nova and can be applied to the federal text once it is released.

items.title: Low-Carbohydrate, Animal-Centered Diets and Plant-Based Diets Exert Opposing Effects on Cardiometabolic Diseases.
items.abstract: Low-carbohydrate, animal-centered (LCAC) diets are promoted for the prevention and treatment of type 2 diabetes (T2D) and cardiovascular disease (CVD) because randomized trials have shown short-term reductions in select risk factors, such as body weight, triglycerides, and glycated hemoglobin. However, controlled feeding studies have shown increases in low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C), apolipoprotein B, and circulating free fatty acids with LCAC diets. Importantly, LCAC diets can also drive lipotoxicity and inflammation. These latter pathological biochemical effects directly act on pathways involved in the development of T2D and CVD. In contrast, high-carbohydrate, unrefined plant-based diets in these conditions reduce insulin requirements even without weight loss, lower blood pressure and medication use, and improve atherogenic lipoproteins and inflammation. Meta-analyses of randomized trials demonstrate reductions in LDL-C, apolipoprotein B, and glycated hemoglobin with vegetarian or vegan diets. Further, plant-based dietary interventions have also shown regression of coronary atherosclerosis and improvements in myocardial perfusion and cardiac function, an effect absent from LCAC diet literature. Thus, public health efforts aimed at the prevention and treatment of T2D and CVD should continue to focus on improving the quantity and quality of plant foods consumed rather than carbohydrate restriction alone.

items.title: Adding Locally Available Foods to SQ-LNS Increased Nutrient Intake but Not the Proportion of Infants Meeting Nutrient Requirements in Rural Zimbabwe: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
items.abstract: Small-quantity lipid-based nutrient supplements (SQ-LNS) improve linear growth but may not close all nutrient gaps. Whether locally available foods can help meet these gaps remains uncertain. Compare infant and young child feeding (IYCF) (ground maize+SQ-LNS) versus "IYCF-plus" (pro-vitamin A maize, SQ-LNS, moringa, egg and sugar beans) on the proportion of infants meeting nutrient requirements. Infants in rural Zimbabwe were randomized to IYCF or IYCF-plus from age 6mo. The primary outcome was the proportion meeting energy requirements at age 9mo using 24-hour dietary recalls. Secondary outcomes were proportion of children meeting protein, iron, zinc, and folate intakes, plus anthropometric indices and hemoglobin concentration. Tertiary outcomes were protein-quality indicators. Analyses used intention-to-treat mixed-effects logistic and linear regression. Among 192 infants (95 IYCF; 97 IYCF-plus), 9 exited and 2 died. At 9 months, 92.2% (95% CI 87.2, 97.2) in the IYCF arm and 92.5% (95% CI 87.9, 97.0) in the IYCF-plus arm met energy requirements (adjusted OR 1.0; 95% CI 0.3, 3.3). Protein adequacy was 100.0% versus 99.3%; iron adequacy was 84.4% versus 88.8%; zinc adequacy was 87.0% versus 93.0%; and folate adequacy was 97.7% versus 96.0%. Anthropometry and haemoglobin concentration showed no evidence of differences: LAZ mean difference -0.0 (95% CI -0.3, 0.2); WAZ -0.1 (-0.4, 0.2); WLZ -0.2 (-0.5, 0.2); haemoglobin concentration -0.0 (-0.3, 0.3). Protein-quality indicators were higher in the IYCF-plus arm than in the IYCF arm, including available protein (mean difference 2.3 g/kg; 95% CI 1.8, 2.8), Digestible Indispensable Amino Acid Score (DIAAS) (mean difference 79.7; 95% CI 68.9, 90.5), and all available amino acids. IYCF-plus using locally available foods plus SQ-LNS did not improve the proportion of infants meeting nutrient requirements more than SQ-LNS+maize alone, but improved protein quality. clinicaltrials.gov NCT04874688.

items.title: Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda at day 100: an ESCMID Emerging Infections Subcommittee update.
items.abstract: The 2026 Bundibugyo virus disease (BVD) outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and Uganda has challenged epidemic control despite rapid expansion of response capacity. To reassess the threats identified by the ESCMID Emerging Infections Subcommittee at day 100 and identify clinical and public-health priorities. This narrative update draws on published literature and WHO, Africa CDC, ECDC, and national public health reports, using 22 August 2026 as the day-100 analytical cut-off, with data through 20 October for a subsequent update. By 22 August, the DRC had reported 5514 confirmed cases and 2642 deaths in 57 health zones across six provinces, making it the largest recorded outbreak in the DRC and the second-largest Ebola outbreak by confirmed case count. Uganda contained 20 cases, and its outbreak was declared over on 27 August. By 20 October, the DRC had reported 9704 cases and 4687 deaths in 66 health zones across eight provinces; Kenya had reported nine epidemiologically linked cases and Nigeria one. Contact follow-up improved, but many transmission chains remained unidentified. BDBV-specific diagnostics, therapeutic and post-exposure prophylaxis trials, and vaccine studies expanded, yet no vaccine or virus-specific treatment had demonstrated clinical efficacy. Cross-reactive antibody responses after licensed Ebola vaccination do not establish protection against BDBV. ECDC assessed infection likelihood for EU/EEA residents as very low. Epidemic control requires complete contact tracing complemented by active case-finding, earlier referral, high-quality supportive care, health-worker protection, community engagement, flexible financing and preservation of essential health services.

items.title: Dismissal Policies for Vaccine Delay and Refusal: Experiences among US Primary Care Pediatricians.
items.abstract: As vaccine hesitancy has grown, some pediatric practices implement vaccine dismissal policies in response to families who refuse or delay immunizations. This study aimed to describe the perspectives and practices that underlie dismissal policies by pediatricians. We conducted an exploratory, qualitative study of United States primary care pediatricians. Brief interviews were conducted virtually, with separate semi-structured scripts used for "dismissers" and "non-dismissers." Data were organized into a matrix format for analysis. Between September 2020 and June 2021, 17 pediatrician interviews were conducted, with 16 included in the data analysis. Of these 16 interviews, 9 were dismissers and 7 were non-dismissers. Both dismissers and non-dismissers felt supported in their policy decisions and were guided in these decisions by a strong support for vaccines. Both groups also differentiated between those who staunchly refused vaccines and those who were vaccine hesitant. Pediatricians with dismissal policies reported frustrations with vaccine refusal and conversations with families about vaccinations that seemed fruitless. Non-dismissers emphasized the value of serving all patients and ensuring that all patients had access to good medical care. Both dismissers and non-dismissers encountered similar reasons for vaccine refusal or delay among vaccine-hesitant families, including concerns about vaccine safety and necessity. In this qualitative study of pediatric primary care physicians, we described the themes, many of which are similar between dismissers and non-dismissers, that underlie the decision of whether to dismiss families for vaccine refusal and delay. Future research should investigate the public health impact of these policies.

items.title: Adverse and Positive Childhood Experiences among US Bereaved Youth (2022-2024).
items.abstract: To describe associations of adverse and positive childhood experiences (ACEs and PCEs) and social demographic characteristics with exposure to parent or guardian death among a nationally representative sample of US youth (6-17 years). We pooled cross-sectional data from the 2022-2024 National Survey of Children's Health (N=101,617). We estimated stepwise Poisson and Negative Binomial regression models testing the association of parent or guardian death with ACEs and PCEs accumulation in both the full sample and racial and ethnic stratified subsamples. Approximately 4% of youth experienced parent or guardian death and were disproportionately non-Hispanic Black, Native American/Other Race, or from low-income households. Bereaved youth were more likely to be exposed to all ACEs and less likely to be exposed to the majority of PCEs relative to their non-bereaved counterparts. Youth exposed to parent or guardian death exhibited significantly more ACEs (β = 0.40, IRR = 1.49, SE = 0.03), yet a similar number of PCEs (β = -0.02, IRR = 0.98, SE = 0.01), relative to their non-bereaved peers. The association between parent and guardian death and ACEs was no longer significant among non-Hispanic Black (β = 0.15, IRR = 1.16, SE = 0.08) and Native American/Other Race (β = 0.12, IRR = 1.12, SE = 0.11) youth relative to other racial and ethnic groups. These findings underscore the elevated and unequal exposure of adversity among youth exposed to parent and guardian death. Implications for targeted pediatric supports that address heightened adversities and inequities within this population are discussed.

items.title: Access to School-Based Health Centers and Annual Well-Child Visits Among Medicaid-Insured Adolescents.
items.abstract: School-based health centers (SBHCs) may mitigate barriers to preventive care. Most existing research does not account for potential confounders. We estimate the association between attending a school with an SBHC and receipt of an annual well-child visit. This retrospective cohort study focused on 10- to 18-year-old students in a large urban school district who had not previously attended a school with an SBHC and who were enrolled in an accountable care organization. Children had to be continuously enrolled for three years prior and one year after the start of the school year. The sample contained 5,600 children in 105 schools for 2022-2023 and 5,200 children in 110 schools for 2023-2024. SBHCs were located in 11 schools. The outcome analyzed was the receipt of a well-child visit within 12 months of the start of the school year. We relied on propensity score-based analyses and inverse probability treatment weighting (IPTW) to estimate average treatment effects for each year. In 2022-2023, 521 students (9.3%) attended a school with an SBHC; in 2023-2024, 789 (15.2%). Attending a school with an SBHC was associated with higher levels of annual well-child visits in both years (5.89 percentage points; p=0.020, 95% CI: 0.92 to 10.85 and 7.33 percentage points; p=0.001, 95% CI: 2.87 to 11.79). Results were consistent across robustness checks. Among Medicaid-insured youth, attending a school with an SBHC was associated with higher rates of completed well-child visits. Expanding SBHC access may improve access to preventive care for adolescents.

items.title: Trajectories of Antibiotic Consumption and Associations with Resistance Across Hospitals and Primary Care: A Population-Level Ecological Study in Shandong Province, China, 2012-2024.
items.abstract: To examine antibiotic consumption patterns and their associations with resistance in hospitals and primary healthcare facilities (PHFs) in Shandong Province to inform antimicrobial stewardship (AMS). Yearly antibiotic consumption (2012-2024) and resistance (2014-2024) data for six resistance phenotypes were obtained in Shandong (population >100 million). Antibiotics were classified using the WHO Anatomical Therapeutic Chemical and AWaRe classification, with expressed as defined daily doses per 1,000 inhabitants per day (DID) and per 1,000 patient visits per day. Consumption structure was assessed using the Shannon index and Gini coefficient. Associations with resistance were examined using Spearman's rank correlation. Total antibiotic consumption decreased by 17.7%, from 11.98 DID in 2012 to 9.86 DID in 2024. Both hospitals and PHFs showed declining diversity and increasing concentration of consumption. Hospitals accounted for 27.7% of total antibiotic consumption, with increasing intensity and a shift towards fluoroquinolones and third-generation cephalosporins, whereas PHFs showed a marked decline and a shift towards extended-spectrum penicillins. Access antibiotics accounted for 27.0% in hospitals and 46.5% in PHFs in 2024. Ecological analyses showed broadly aligned consumption-resistance trends in PHFs, but divergent associations in hospitals. Antibiotic consumption declined in Shandong during a period of sustained AMS policies, but trends differed across healthcare settings. The alignment between primary care consumption and hospital-based resistance suggests that antibiotic use in PHFs may represent an important component of regional antimicrobial resistance dynamics. Future stewardship efforts should integrate consumption, resistance, and prescribing data to guide targeted interventions.

items.title: Very High Baseline HIV-RNA and Advanced HIV Disease: Outcomes After INSTI-Based ART Initiation in the ICONA cohort.
items.abstract: To evaluate virological suppression (VS) and clinical outcome among ART-naïve people with HIV (PWH) initiating integrase inhibitor (INSTI)-based antiretroviral therapy, according to advanced HIV disease (AHD) status and baseline HIV-RNA. We included ART-naïve PWH enrolled in the ICONA cohort between 2018 and 2024 who started an INSTI-based regimen. Participants were stratified by baseline HIV-RNA (<100,000, 100,000-499,999, and ≥500,000 copies/mL) and AHD status (CD4 <200 cells/mm³ and/or AIDS). Time to VS (HIV-RNA <50 copies/mL) and to composite clinical endpoint (new AIDS, major cardio-cerebrovascular events, cancer, or death) were evaluated by Kaplan-Meier. The associations of AHD and outcomes, with effect modification by baseline HIV-RNA stratum, were evaluated by Cox model adjusting for confounders. Among 4,150 PWH, 1,733 (41.8%) had AHD. The longest time to VS occurred in those with HIV-RNA ≥500,000 copies/mL: 7.2 (6.6-7.8) versus 5.8 (5.1-6.6) months in PWH with and without AHD, with a 12 and 24 months' VS probabilities of 69.8% versus 77.9% and 88.9% versus 91.4%, respectively. AHD was associated with lower hazard of VS across all HIV-RNA strata (<100,000 aHR 0.87 [95% CI 0.77-0.98]; 100,000-499,999 aHR 0.81 [95% CI 0.72-0.91]; ≥500,000 aHR 0.82 [95% CI 0.72-0.95]). AHD was associated with higher hazard of clinical endpoints as HIV-RNA increased [from aHR 4.94 (95% CI 3.29-7.42) <100,000 to aHR 6.51 (95% CI 3.30-12.84) ≥500,000]. AHD was consistently associated with delayed VS and worse clinical outcome, particularly among PWH with very high HIV-RNA at ART initiation.

items.title: Examining the intersection of extreme heat exposures, social determinants of health, and adverse pregnancy outcomes: a scoping review.
items.abstract: Extreme heat exposure during pregnancy is associated with adverse pregnancy outcomes (APOs), complications themselves linked to long-term maternal cardiovascular risk, and these effects appear to vary by social and environmental context (e.g., neighborhood deprivation, greenness, and rural-urban residence). We describe the U.S. evidence and characterize how social determinants of health (SDoH), particularly area-level measures, are defined in this literature. PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science Core Collection were searched through July 14, 2025, plus secondary searches in September 2025. We included U.S.-focused empirical epidemiologic studies and evidence syntheses that (1) assessed extreme heat exposure in pregnancy; (2) incorporated at least one individual- or area-level SDoH as exposure, covariate, or effect modifier; and (3) reported at least one APO, from preterm birth, low birth weight, stillbirth, hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, and gestational diabetes to composite APOs, severe maternal morbidity, and acute cardiovascular events. Two reviewers independently screened records; a senior reviewer resolved conflicts. Data were extracted into standardized forms and synthesized narratively. Per scoping review guidance, formal risk-of-bias assessment was not performed. We included 37 studies (28 empirical and 9 reviews). Heat exposure was typically defined using percentile-based thresholds (most commonly the 90th or 95th local percentile), heat-wave definitions, apparent-temperature metrics, or absolute cutoffs, with the week before delivery the most frequent window. Preterm birth was the most evaluated outcome, followed by birthweight-related outcomes and stillbirth. Individual-level socioeconomic measures (e.g., education, insurance) appeared in nearly all empirical studies, whereas area-level measures-neighborhood income or poverty, deprivation indices, greenness or tree canopy, heat-trapping land cover, region, and rural-urban residence-appeared in fewer than half. Five of 12 studies incorporating area-level SDoH reported stronger heat-APO associations in disadvantaged or lower-greenness settings. Examples include heat-associated stillbirth risk only in the most deprived neighborhoods; heat-preterm birth associations strongest where both greenness and socioeconomic status were low; and stronger heat-gestational diabetes associations with lower greenness. U.S. studies reported associations between extreme heat in pregnancy and multiple APOs. Area-level SDoH and environmental context were inconsistently incorporated. Standardized use of place-based measures may better identify communities most vulnerable to heat and inform equity-focused, climate-resilient maternal health research and action. Heat exposure in pregnancy is linked to adverse outcomes, and risk may be higher in neighborhoods experiencing socioeconomic deprivation, highlighting the need to measure area-level social determinants in climate-maternal health research.

items.title: Genomic Characterization of a Typical Enteropathogenic Escherichia coli Isolate from an Egyptian Fruit Bat, Rousettus aegyptiacus from Coastal Kenya
items.abstract: Enteropathogenic Escherichia coli (EPEC) are responsible for significant morbidity and mortality cases among young children under the age of five, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. Atypical EPEC has frequently been reported from animal hosts, however, information on the occurrence and genomic characteristics of typical EPEC in wildlife reservoirs remains limited. This study characterized an Escherichia coli isolated from an Egyptian fruit bat (Rousettus aegyptiacus) sampled in coastal Kenya using whole-genome sequencing. Oral and rectal swabs were collected from 24 bats captured in Kikambala, Kilifi County, Kenya. Bacterial isolates were cultured, sequenced on the Illumina NextSeq 1000 platform, and analyzed using a bioinformatics workflow that included in silico taxonomic classification, serotyping and multilocus sequence typing, virulence gene profiling, antimicrobial resistance gene detection, plasmid identification, and core genome phylogenetic analysis. One isolate, KIKB-471-SWR-A (O128:H6; ST15625), was classified as typical EPEC. Genomic analysis confirmed the characteristic virulence architecture of typical EPEC. Despite numerous antimicrobial resistance-associated genes being detected, the isolate remained phenotypically susceptible to all antimicrobials tested. The isolate clustered within an EPEC lineage, closely associated with a human-derived EPEC strain, and genetically distinct from both commensal and laboratory E. coli reference strains. Despite no evidence of zoonotic transmission, the findings demonstrated that wildlife can harbor E. coli lineages possessing virulence determinants associated with human pathogenic EPEC strains, underscoring the importance of genomic surveillance at wildlife?human interfaces within a One Health framework to improve the understanding of ecology, evolution, and public health significance of diarrheagenic E. coli.

items.title: GA-NIFS: A post-starburst main sequence disk galaxy undergoing ordered rotation at z = 4.26
items.abstract: Rotating galaxies with relaxed gaseous disks have been discovered across cosmic time, from the local Universe to high redshift. But few such sources have been confirmed at z > 4, making them a precious sample to examine the conditions required for such ordered kinematics in an early, more chaotic Universe. One of the best examples of this sample is the galaxy $\rm DLA0817g1$ (z = 4.2603), which shows remarkably clear rotation in ALMA [C ii] data. We present JWST/NIRSpec IFU data (R ∼ 2700) of $\rm DLA0817g1$, which we combine with archival ALMA [C ii] observations to place constraints on its ISM conditions and morpho-kinematics. From a combination of line ratios, we find a high gas-phase metallicity (Zgas ∼ 0.8 Z⊙), high fraction of obscured star formation, low ionisation (compared to other high-redshift galaxies observed with JWST), and no significant evidence for AGN. Dynamical modelling with $\rm ^{3D}$Barolo reveals nearly identical rotation in $\rm H\alpha$ and [C ii]. Using our metallicity estimate and previous CO and [C ii] detections, we derive a new estimate of the molecular gas mass, relieving a previous strain in the mass budget. Altogether, we suggest that this is a post-burst, main-sequence galaxy, where high levels of past star formation resulted in significant chemical enrichment (i.e., Zgas and Mdust), but the current activity is lower (i.e., lower ionisation parameter and lack of starburst activity). These new observations have opened a window into the interplay of gas, metallicity, star formation, and kinematics in a prototypical early disk galaxy.

items.title: The nature of the Norma arm as a bar-driven star-forming shock front
items.abstract: The Milky Way is commonly depicted as having four main spiral arms, including the Norma–outer arm, and a central stellar bar whose properties remain debated. Masers associated with young high-mass stars have been used to trace a segment of the ‘Norma arm’ extending from one end of the Galaxy’s central stellar bar. Recent work suggests that these masers may reside along a spiral arm or occupy the dominant x 1 stellar orbits that give the bar its shape. Here we use a new generation of N -body, hydrodynamic simulations to argue that these million-year-old masers instead trace the Galactic bar’s quadrant I shock front or, equivalently, its dust lane. This implies that the bar dust lane is star-forming, shedding new light on our understanding of star formation processes in the Milky Way. By associating the masers with the simulated shock front, we determine the parameters of the bar to be: a ≈ 4.3 ± 0.2 kpc, b ≈ 2.3 ± 0.2 kpc, ϕ = $${{20}_{-2}^{+5}}^{\circ }$$ 20 - 2 + 5 ∘ and Ω p ≲ 40 km s −1 kpc −1 , representing the semimajor and semiminor half-lengths of the bar, the inclination angle and the pattern speed, respectively. This raises questions about the Milky Way’s spiral structure and suggests that the Galactic bar is long, slow and star-forming.

items.title: Optimal Linear Regression Without a Variance
items.abstract: We study high-probability linear regression in the infinite variance regime, wherecthe regression noise has only a finite conditional $α$-moment $ν$ for some unknown $α\in(1,2)$, and the covariates may only have finite moments up to a given order (e.g., 4th moment). We give a black-box reduction that converts finite-variance regression procedures into weak-moment procedures. The reduction is based on empirical residual pruning and is agnostic to the moment exponent, the noise scale, the covariance, and the design moment. Under a finite fourth-moment condition on the covariates, any finite-variance subroutine attaining the sub-Gaussian rate yields the following when the number of samples $n$ is above a suitably defined threshold: Without knowing $α$ or $ν$, we have with probability at least $1-δ$ that $ \|\widehatθ-θ^*\|_Σ \lesssim_α ν^{1/α} \big(\frac{d+\log(1/δ)}{n}\big)^{\frac{α-1}α}, $ where $d$ is the dimension, $Σ$ is the covariate covariance matrix, and $\|v\|_Σ:=(v^\topΣv)^{1/2}$. We further prove a matching minimax lower bound that holds under the same conditions. The reduction is computationally efficient whenever the finite-variance subroutine is. We also obtain a distribution-free prediction guarantee under a bounded raw $α$-moment assumption on the response, and give an analogous $α$-agnostic reduction for mean estimation.

items.title: Non-penetrating World Models
items.abstract: We study a new problem of preventing object penetration in interactive video world models. To understand how existing models handle this, we introduce NoPeBench, a benchmark that evaluates how world models respond to physical obstacles. Our evaluation reveals that none of the open-source models can reliably prevent such failures. Surprisingly, however, these models already encode the information needed to predict such violations. We find that the hidden states of diffusion transformers (DiTs) can predict whether a candidate action will penetrate an obstacle. Building on this, we introduce NoPeWorld, a lightweight framework that detects and prevents penetration. Specifically, we train a small prediction head on top of a frozen DiT's hidden states to read out if a candidate action is safe or not. Unsafe actions are then replaced with safe ones that best preserve the original intent. Despite its simplicity, NoPeWorld substantially reduces the physical violation rate, averaged over six video world models, from 74% to 16%. Remarkably, our method shows zero-shot generalization to open-domain imagery, third-person viewpoints, and moving obstacles. We publicly release our code, the NoPeBench benchmark, and model weights. Project Page: https://nopeworld.github.io .

items.title: Model Carving: Training Transformers That Optimize Their Own Topology
items.abstract: Machine learning has largely kept separate the choice of architecture and the process of training. A classic Transformer, for instance, trains a fixed set of attention and MLP sublayers at every layer, in the same order, and optimizes the weights within. This uniformity is a convention rather than a principled design choice, and it is likely suboptimal: the best architecture for a given task may be smaller, more efficient, and far from uniform. We believe that, ideally, training itself should shape the model's topology. To this end, we introduce Model Carving, which learns both a Transformer's weights and its architecture in a single run. By applying learnable, scalar gates to each sublayer, we allow the training loss to remove the model's own components during training -- freeing a smaller heterogeneous network inside. We evaluate Model Carving by pre-training standard Transformers from 140M to 2.7B parameters and looped Transformers from 140M to 1.3B. At equal training compute, carved models reach a lower validation loss than dense models trained with up to 1.7 times more compute. Furthermore, carved models also outperform size-matched models produced by pruning or distillation, suggesting that the best way to obtain small models for edge devices is to carve them during training, not to compress a large one afterwards. This advantage both grows with scale and carries over to downstream tasks such as few-shot evaluation and generation. Because the removed sublayers no longer run, carved models also cost up to 34% fewer FLOPs per token and decode up to 1.6 times faster without cost in quality. Our results show that architecture, like weights, should be learned and not fixed in advance, and that inside every large transformer is a smaller, faster, stronger one waiting to be carved out.

items.title: BioEmu2: Scalable Emulation of Biomolecular Dynamics
items.abstract: Despite major advances in structure prediction, modelling the motions and interactions that drive biomolecular function at scale remains a central challenge. We introduce BioEmu2, a generative model for atomically resolved biomolecular structures combining static structure prediction, equilibrium sampling and time evolution, that samples orders of magnitude faster than molecular dynamics (MD). Trained on experimental and synthetic structures and extensive MD data, it supports multi-component systems containing proteins, nucleic acids, modified residues, ligands and ions. Structure-prediction accuracy is comparable to top open-weight biomolecular folding models, and a context parallel mode enables prediction of megadalton complexes. Equilibrium distributions approximate MD references with free-energy errors near 1 kcal/mol across tested proteins and complexes. Time propagation predicts long-timescale dynamical trajectories and kinetics of binding and conformational changes. Generated structures can be controlled by conditioning on residue contacts or steering with user-defined bias potentials. Enhanced sampling enables free energy calculation involving rare states. BioEmu2 makes the study of biomolecular ensembles and dynamics scalable.

items.title: SUAF: Spectral Universal Advantage Features for Zero-Shot Policy Improvement
items.abstract: Reward-independent representations enable reinforcement learning agents to reuse knowledge across tasks, but limited representation capacity raises three fundamental questions: what statistical dependence should these representations capture, which components of that dependence should be retained for policy improvement, and how does discarding the remaining components affect decision-making? We address these questions through canonical dependence analysis. For a reference policy, we construct an action-centered, positive-lag canonical dependence matrix (CDM) that isolates the additional predictive contribution of the current action beyond the current state. Its singular value decomposition yields Spectral Universal Advantage Features (SUAF), paired features that recover delayed advantage through linear reward projections. We show that the spectrum quantifies mutual information between current action and future state-action visitation conditioned on current state and determines reward specific approximation errors. Retaining the leading modes gives optimal rank-constrained approximations under both isotropic average-case and reward-uniform minimax criteria. Separating the immediate reward contrast also avoids the spectral floor arising from direct compression of the full advantage operator. To learn SUAF from reward-free data, we develop an action-centered Soft-HGR objective with bidirectional temporal-difference estimation. We further connect spectral approximation errors to sufficient conditions for policy improvement. Finite-state experiments validate the spectral predictions and feature-learning method, while zero-shot evaluations on discrete tasks and continuous-control benchmarks demonstrate the utility of the learned representations across rewards.

items.title: StereoVLM: Binocular Vision-Language Models for Metric 3D Spatial Reasoning
items.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) exhibit strong semantic understanding but remain limited in their ability to reason about metric 3D space in the physical world. Existing VLMs typically infer 3D scene structure from one or more images without known camera calibration or cross-view geometric constraints. This makes metric 3D inference inherently ambiguous and leaves it unclear whether their spatial predictions are grounded in visual evidence or driven primarily by semantic priors. In contrast, calibrated stereo provides explicit cross-view geometry that resolves this ambiguity and offers a more reliable foundation for metric 3D perception and geometric generalization. We investigate how VLMs can learn transferable 3D representations directly from calibrated binocular observations. To this end, we introduce StereoVLM, the first geometry-aware binocular VLM for metric 3D spatial reasoning. StereoVLM follows a hierarchical learning paradigm spanning from cross-view correspondence and disparity estimation to calibration-conditioned metric depth perception and semantic spatial reasoning. We further find that disparity supervision generalizes substantially better than direct binocular depth supervision on unseen environments. To evaluate these capabilities, we introduce Stereo3D-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark across three levels, from point-level geometry to object-level spatial reasoning. StereoVLM-8B achieves 95.17% depth accuracy ($δ_1$) and a 66.98 average object-level score on Stereo3D-Bench. Intervention results further indicate that the model's performance on Stereo3D-Bench benefits from valid cross-view geometry and cannot be explained solely by additional visual tokens or semantic priors. Hierarchical geometric supervision also yields average gains of 3.54 points across five spatial benchmarks and 4.3 percentage points in RoboCasa manipulation success.

items.title: Star Panoptic Quality: Selectively Evaluating Split and Merged Instances
items.abstract: Detecting individual instances is crucial for many segmentation problems. However, expert instance annotations are often unavailable, so instances are approximated heuristically (e.g., as connected components of semantic maps), which can merge touching objects or split fragmented ones. Even when expert annotations exist, expert disagreement or structural delineation biases can yield split or merged reference instances, corresponding to over- or under-segmentation, respectively. Panoptic Quality (PQ) and related metrics capture both segmentation and detection quality while weighting all instances equally, regardless of size. Yet when the references are biased, these metrics can neither detect split or merged instances nor distinguish valid from invalid overor under-segmentation. We present Star Panoptic Quality (StarPQ), a novel evaluation ramework, which closes this gap in two steps: First, we construct a so-called star forest in the bipartite graph whose clean, merge, and split stars isolate different failure modes. Second, we calculate the final metric by individually weighting each failure mode, allowing practitioners to account for instance delineation biases. Across various experiments, we demonstrate that StarPQ not only enables targeted penalization or eniency towards specific failure modes, but also serves as a diagnostic tool to reveal their prevalence.

items.title: Functional Depth Is Learned: Isolating the Computation That Layers Produce Only Together
items.abstract: Transformer performance scales with depth, but layer count merely counts the opportunities for sequential computation: layers could still behave as nearly independent refinements that barely depend on one another. We study how transformers develop functional depth during pretraining, introducing an exact inclusion-exclusion decomposition that isolates the connected component, i.e., the computation that appears only when a specified set of layers acts together under identity ablation. Tracking this quantity across public checkpoints of Pythia, OLMo, and Amber yields three findings. First, write-relative connected coordination strengthens from its initialization or earliest-checkpoint baseline as pretraining proceeds, across all measured interaction orders. Second, these connected components are behaviorally consequential under direct intervention: deleting them damages perplexity more than deleting a norm-matched random direction at the same site in all 35 measured model-order cells. Third, pairwise representation similarity is consistently negatively correlated with pairwise connected coordination across seven models, yet the two signals are not interchangeable: similarity- and coordination-based block-removal criteria often agree in Pythia but diverge on Amber. Together, these results suggest that architectural depth provides the opportunity for sequential computation, while pretraining progressively organizes cross-layer dependencies within that depth.

items.title: Decision Columns as an Index: Interpretable Embeddings for Explainable Entity Matching and Search
items.abstract: Business data systems must determine whether records refer to the same entity and retrieve records satisfying requests whose decisive properties are implicit. As agents act on these records, both tasks require auditable reasons. Dense embeddings perform well but offer opaque coordinates, cannot be filtered by meaning, and require corpus re-encoding to add new properties. We propose interpretable embeddings built from decision columns: each column stores a decision model's calibrated answer to a natural-language question, with outcomes yes, no, or not stated. A record's embedding is its answers across an ordered set of questions. Similarity decomposes exactly into per-question contributions, and new questions add coordinates without altering existing ones. On public product benchmarks, question-space retrieval matches dense candidate generation statistically in a retrieve-then-verify entity matcher, while providing exact explanations for accepted matches. Questions derived from retrieval failures triple mean reciprocal rank without re-encoding prior answers. For search, inferring the attributes of a suitable result outperforms encoding only the literal request, and combining question-space and dense scores improves retrieval, though not at our prespecified confidence threshold. A single small neural network predicts the full interpretable vector from an existing dense embedding, enabling corpus backfilling from a few thousand labeled rows at roughly 1/200 the cost. We position interpretable embeddings as a complementary, readable retrieval channel for explaining matches, filtering on attributes, and extending indexes as failures expose missing facts.

items.title: The Dual-Tier Sentiment Framework: Scalable Multimodal UX Attribution in Web Search
items.abstract: Sustaining user experience (UX) quality in large-scale web search requires scalable evaluation. Traditional surveys are slow and bottleneck rapid A/B testing, while automated metrics often lack the granularity to diagnose visual-spatial UX anomalies. To address this, we introduce the Dual-Tier Sentiment Framework, a novel industrial architecture for automated UX attribution. Tier 1 (Macro System) acts as a scalable user sentiment regression detector, utilizing a fine-tuned encoder-decoder LLM (based on Gemini XS) on telemetry features. Through multi-task regularization and contextual feature engineering, this tier achieves a +9.8% PR-AUC gain on over 500,000 held-out records, matching baseline recall on all validated regressions with $\sim$20% relative precision gain among the 12 held-out experiments. In production, it reduces measurement latency from weeks to hours and cuts survey overhead by over 40%. Tier 2 (Micro System) provides granular diagnostics by employing a Multimodal LLM (Gemini 3.0 Pro) to natively assess visual renderings and spatial layout of web result blocks, quantifying "User Toil" as the estimated effort required to reach a satisfactory result. Enhanced by RL-based automated prompt optimization and an AI judge for win/loss patterns, the MLLM yields a $>$6.5% F1 score improvement, offering deep insights into content quality and layout friction. Ultimately, this framework enables scalable, accurate, and diagnostic UX attribution, processing O(100k) live experiment queries daily.

items.title: TEA-Bench-BR: Can Coding Agents Turn a Branching Clinical Specification into Correct Code?
items.abstract: Coding agents increasingly implement rules written by domain experts, and bugs in such code are silent: it runs and returns a plausible answer. We introduce TEA-Bench-BR, a benchmark built on the Brazilian pathway for early autism (TEA) screening: three fictitious instruments with the structure of real ones, a multi-professional referral flow, and export to FHIR R4 with the national RNDS profiles, all specified in Portuguese. A generator samples each task's parameters (144 tasks, 6,798 hidden cases), and the hidden cases kill all 1,955 non-equivalent mutants of the reference. With Gemma 4 as the agent, the 12B solves 38.0% of single-instrument tasks and none at the FHIR level; the 31B solves 77.8%, 85.2% and 78.7% at levels 1 to 3 and passes over 99% of the hidden cases, its remaining failures mostly in input validation rather than clinical decisions. With the same tasks in English, the 31B solves 57.4% at level 3, as its code validates an identifier less often; the 12B's, more often. The 12B misses 10.10% of the cases that call for referral; the 31B, 0.02%. A contamination probe on a modified PHQ-9 finds no error that follows the original rules.

items.title: Speculative Decoding Is Less Speculative Than You Think
items.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates language-model inference by preparing candidate continuations before the target model generates them. Its efficiency depends on how well limited drafting computation anticipates the path the target will actually follow. Anticipating this path involves two sources of uncertainty: the target model's predictions and the randomness of sampling. Yet the former requires a target-model forward pass, while the latter can be fixed before drafting. Building on this observation, we introduce DICE (Draw-Informed Candidate Selection), which pre-samples and synchronizes verification randomness across drafting and verification. By combining these known draws with predictions from an existing drafter, DICE allocates computation toward continuations more likely to be used in the current sampling run. This principle guides node selection throughout draft-tree construction and extends to asynchronous prefetching, where DICE predicts which next-round drafts to prepare. Without additional drafter training or changes to the target sampling distribution, DICE achieves state-of-the-art decoding throughput across diverse settings, with speedups of up to 24.6pp over strong baselines.

items.title: LesionAgent: Training-Free Agentic Tumor Tracking and Response Assessment in Longitudinal CT
items.abstract: Every few months, a cancer patient's CT scans decide whether treatment continues. 3D foundation models can now detect, segment, register and track lesions, yet none of them reads the scans as a radiologist does. A radiologist decides which findings are lesions, which are the same lesion months later and whether a new spot means progression, and checks each decision against the extensive rules of a clinical guideline. We introduce LesionAgent, an LLM agent that performs this read end to end without task-specific training. It operates frozen 3D models as tools, acts in 3D through coordinate-labelled views, remembers every lesion across visits in a registry, verifies every model output it relies on, and leaves every number to a deterministic guideline engine. On four public longitudinal CT datasets, LesionAgent tracks more lesions and measures them more accurately than every automatic baseline, and where the same 3D models chained by fixed rules call progression falsely at 33 of 56 follow-ups, it does so twice. On clinical follow-up CTs, it agrees with the radiologists' response at 20 of 23 follow-ups, including every change in response, and without training on DeepLesion, it retrieves more of its lesions than every tracker trained on it (89.0% vs. 87.4%). Its harness, not its LLM, makes the difference: given the same LLM and 3D models but not the harness, Claude Code reaches a detection F1 of 41% and LesionAgent 78%, and an open-weight LLM that can run inside the hospital rises from 6% to 73%. LesionAgent and a napari reading app for any LLM are available at https://github.com/MIC-DKFZ/LesionAgent.

items.title: Beyond Visual Fidelity: Comparing Categorical and Continuous World Models
items.abstract: Visual world models can now generate compelling interactive worlds, but visual realism does not guarantee faithful dynamics. We systematically compare how categorical and continuous prediction shape learned dynamics under both next-token and iterative whole-frame generation. These choices are often bundled in approaches such as autoregressive token models and whole-frame flow matching. We design controlled 2D and 3D environments and evaluate dynamics validity, calibration, and visual quality. In 2D with lossless visual encoding, categorical models achieve higher rollout validity with less training compute, particularly for stochastic entities. Among categorical models, greedy decoding produces the highest rollout validity, while sampling from a next-token model yields the best-calibrated stochastic predictions. Failures in continuous models, such as disappearing game characters, echo those seen in more complex environments. Here, known dynamics let us measure their impact. In 3D, categorical models also achieve stronger long-horizon performance with less training compute. Even models with lossy tokenization remain competitive on semantic accuracy and FVD, despite lower next-frame RGB accuracy. Together, these findings make a strong case for categorical prediction as a compute-efficient route to learning world dynamics.

items.title: Integrating Generative Artificial Intelligence with Learning Style Models: Opportunities, Challenges, and Future Directions
items.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (Generative AI) has emerged as a powerful tool for transforming learning. This review examines how Generative AI can be integrated with established learning style models (VARK, Kolb, Felder-Silverman, and Honey & Mumford) to support student engagement in large online classes. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, we searched Scopus, IEEE Xplore, and Google Scholar (2015 to 2026) and included 41 studies that met the eligibility criteria. The review maps Generative AI capabilities to learning style preferences, synthesizes existing implementations, highlights benefits and challenges, and proposes pathways for future research and practice. Despite ongoing debates regarding the empirical validity of learning styles, Generative AI enables flexible, multimodal, and real-time adaptation. This study offers practical insights for educators and developers seeking to build more effective, learner centered learning systems

items.title: SLICR: Strategy Logic-Guided Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
items.abstract: Specification-guided reinforcement learning (RL) translates formal specifications of desired behavior of agents into shaped rewards. This paper introduces SLICR, a significant paradigm shift that advances the state of the art to specification-guided RL in adversarial settings under partial observability. We employ Strategy Logic (SL), which allows explicit quantification over agents' strategies and uses the linear temporal logic (LTL) to specify the agents' objectives and constraints. This enables reasoning not only about how agents should act to satisfy a specification, but also about how they should respond to the strategies and behaviors of other agents. We evaluate SLICR on three popular benchmarks: Predator-Prey, Google Research Football, and our home-grown extension of SMAC-HARD, demonstrating its effectiveness, scalability, and ability to adapt to diverse adversarial strategies.

items.title: Who Grades the Agent? Privilege Separation for Coding-Agent Benchmarks
items.abstract: Benchmarks for AI-based coding agents are a staple of the current AI landscape, because they are the leading way to measure the performance of LLMs. Their scores guide business and research decisions. Evaluating coding agents is challenging, since they are able to manipulate their evaluation infrastructure to artificially achieve better scores. Grading an agent's solution often requires running its code, which can then manipulate the evaluation process. BenchJack, an automated benchmark auditor, recently reached near-perfect scores on nine of ten popular agent benchmarks without actually solving their tasks. Agents already do this unprompted, as OpenAI's July 2026 Hugging Face incident showed. Building on secure systems design, we introduce SplitBench, a privilege separation framework for evaluating coding agents and the first in the scientific literature to separate running a task's tests from judging their results. Even an agent whose code takes over the entire test environment cannot forge a pass, because a trusted grader holds the expected answers. We show that real-world benchmarks (e.g., Terminal-Bench, DeepSWE) can be ported to the SplitBench framework with minimal effort and high fidelity: 180 of 202 tasks convert, and SplitBench agrees with the native graders on 98.7% of agent attempts. We attack the converted tasks in the worst case, where adversarial agents can read all the grading code but not the expected answers. SplitBench blocked 75% of their attempts; the rest mostly reveal weaknesses in the original tasks' tests rather than flaws in SplitBench.

items.title: Beyond Self-Critique: Epistemic Convergence Control for Multi-Agent Research Verification
items.abstract: Multi-agent systems for scientific claim verification increasingly rely on role-structured LLM debate to pressure-test hypotheses. However, when debating agents are instantiated from the same underlying base model, they share identical latent representations, making self-critique bias structurally inevitable. Static fixed-iteration protocols compound this by either halting prematurely before evidence stabilizes or wasting inference compute after convergence. We present \sys{}, a multi-agent research verification framework that addresses both failure modes. First, we introduce an asymmetric role architecture comprising an Advocate, Skeptic, and Arbitrator with opposing epistemic directives, producing significantly lower role-embedding similarity (0.852 vs.\ 0.918 for symmetric Multi-Agent Debate [MAD], $p = 5.82 \times 10^{-8}$) and surfacing more contested claims (22.0\% vs.\ 15.4\%). Second, we propose the Belief-Delta ($\DB$) convergence criterion, an evidence-grounded stopping rule that eliminates over-iteration (0.0\% vs.\ 62.5\% for Fixed-$3$) while cutting LLM calls by 2.4$\times$. Third, each supported claim is anchored to a verbatim literature snippet audited by an independent NLI classifier, achieving a 21.7\% hallucination rate (comparable to 25.9\% for a Self-Refine critic, $p = 0.61$) while establishing auditable evidence grounding. Across 200 runs on 40 research hypotheses evaluated with DeepSeek-R1-32B, \sys{} balances compute efficiency with rigorous epistemic verification.

items.title: Auditable Financial Knowledge Graphs: Schema-Driven Construction and Intrinsic Quality Evaluation
items.abstract: Financial documents combine narrative disclosures, accounting metrics, corporate structures, management commentary, and time-dependent facts, making them difficult to represent using conventional chunk-based retrieval-augmented generation systems. This paper presents an auditable, schema-driven methodology for constructing temporal financial knowledge graphs from page-delimited documents parsed using a general purpose document intelligence service. Overlapping document windows undergo phased large language model extraction of structural entities, quantitative observations, and domain-specific relationships. Candidate graph elements are validated against predefined schemas and consolidated through scope-aware exact, normalized, fuzzy, embedding-based, and LLM-assisted entity resolution. Temporal merge constraints, deterministic edge deduplication, conflict-aware property management, and fine-grained provenance preserve issuer identity, reporting-period validity, and traceability to source evidence. The contributions of this work comprise the proposed methodology for financial knowledge graph construction, the creation of an evidence-grounded temporal knowledge graph from heterogeneous financial documents, and an intrinsic framework for evaluating the quality of the resulting graph. The evaluation framework assesses seven weighted dimensions, two hard validation gates, and structural diagnostics. By separating graph-quality assessment from downstream retrieval and answer generation, the framework supports systematic diagnosis and iterative refinement of the constructed graph.

items.title: Graph Signal Generation via Graph-Aware Diffusion Models
items.abstract: Many signals are defined on the nodes of a graph, such as traffic flow at road sensors or user purchases of related products. They are often partly observed, and learning their distribution enables imputing missing values and forecasting future ones. Diffusion models learn such distributions, but their forward noise is independent across nodes and does not depend on the graph. We introduce graph-aware diffusion (GAD), whose forward process is a heat diffusion on the graph driven by Gaussian noise. In the graph Fourier basis, the forward transition is a scalar Gaussian channel at each frequency. With a shared diffusion rate, high graph frequencies are attenuated faster than low ones. We propose Mode-Adaptive SNR Scheduling (MASS), which assigns each graph frequency its own diffusion rate and keeps all of them at the same SNR. For graph-stationary signals, MASS equalizes the normalized error of the optimal linear denoiser across frequencies. We bound reverse-SDE stiffness as a function of the (shifted) Laplacian's condition number, with a logarithmic upper bound for MASS and a linear lower bound for shared rates. GAD with MASS improves recommendation accuracy by 5-19%, reduces traffic-imputation RMSE by up to 7.8% with half as many reverse steps, and improves forecasting MAE and RMSE using only 3 reverse steps.

items.title: Redesigning Neural Networks to Not be Confidently Wrong even to Strong Adversarial Attacks
items.abstract: Early deep learning models attempted to simulate visual perception using a neural hierarchy that alternated between two types of layer: one modelled on cortical simple cells (that was designed to increase selectivity), and one modelled on cortical complex cells (that aimed to increase tolerance). We show that such a neural network (NN) architecture, when implemented with novel components that are better able to learn selective and tolerant representations, is capable of accurate and robust image classification and improved alignment between the behaviour of the model and the perceptual abilities of humans. Firstly, the proposed models are shallow, fewer than ten layer-pairs, which is more consistent with the rapid feedforward object categorisation performed by the biological visual system. Secondly, they are far less prone to producing classification predictions with high confidence for samples from unknown classes or for image consisting of pure noise, and hence, like humans are not easily fooled into perceiving objects that are not present in the image. Thirdly, for the proposed NNs adversarial samples cause predictions with low confidence, enabling them to be accurately identified. In contrast to humans, our networks still do not correctly classify adversarial samples. However, the behaviour of our networks is a significant step towards human-like behaviour compared to standard DNNs that produce highly confident, but incorrect, classification predictions for adversarial samples. The increased robustness to adversarial and unknown samples is achieved while maintaining competitive performance in terms of generalisation to novel samples from the training categories. This enables models of this type to be competitive with state-of-the-art DNNs across multiple different evaluation metrics and benchmark tasks.

items.title: SLP-Bench: Evaluating and Improving Acoustic Claims of Reasoning Audio Language Models on Clinical Speech
items.abstract: Audio language models (ALMs) can answer clinical questions from speech, outperforming baselines built on handcrafted acoustic features. Reasoning ALMs generate a chain of thought that refers to properties of the speaker's voice before predicting. Each statement the model makes about the voice needs to be checked against clinicians' perceptual ratings of the same recording. On clinical speech, existing evaluations score only the final answer. We introduce Speech Language Pathologist Bench (SLP-Bench), a benchmark grading each acoustic claim in the chain of thought against clinicians' perceptual ratings of the same recording. It covers five clinician-rated datasets and 25 perceptual dimensions, and assesses claims for factuality, stability under resampling, and consistency across reworded and different questions. Across ten open-weight reasoning ALMs evaluated zero-shot, claim balanced accuracy ranges from 0.52 to 0.58, claims change under resampling and rewording, and the most consistent models are not the most factual. Fine-tuning a 7B ALM with GRPO on a reward for claims that agree with clinicians raises its claim balanced accuracy from 0.54 to 0.60 and its mean kappa from 0.39 to 0.61, while preserving answer accuracy on per-dimension questions. SLP-Bench is available upon request, subject to approval by the providers of each dataset.

items.title: $\mathtt{DistP}$: Scaling Local-Update Training with Zero-Shot Hyperparameter Transfer
items.abstract: Local-update methods offer a communication-efficient alternative to Distributed Data Parallelism ($\mathtt{DDP}$), but introduce additional hyperparameters that require costly tuning. For $\mathtt{DDP}$, zero-shot hyperparameter transfer reduces this cost by reusing settings tuned on smaller models, but its applicability to local-update training remains unclear. We propose $\mathtt{DistP}$, a theoretical framework extending existing transfer rules from $\mathtt{DDP}$ to local-update training with varying worker counts, local steps, and outer optimizers. With averaging as the outer optimizer, $\mathtt{DistP}$ supports learning-rate transfer across width and depth while improving model quality. The tuned inner learning rate also directly transfers across synchronization intervals, but follows two regimes when increasing the global batch size: square-root learning-rate scaling for larger local batches and a fixed reference rate for additional workers. We then generalize width and depth transfer to other outer optimizers, enabling stable scaling with $\mathtt{Adam}$. However, with momentum in the outer optimizer, changing batch size or local steps can require inner--outer learning-rate tuning, consistent with prior work. In language-modeling experiments at $823$M parameters, $\mathtt{DistP}$ reduces validation loss by $8.1\%$ and improves mean downstream accuracy by $10\%$ relative to baselines without retuning at the larger scale. Fitted scaling laws suggest that this advantage grows with the compute budget, reinforcing the benefits of $\mathtt{DistP}$ for communication-efficient training.

items.title: ChildAI-Gov: An Evidence-Linked AI System for Assessing EdTech Policies Against Children's Digital Rights
items.abstract: We present ChildAI-Gov, an explainable AI system for assessing whether education-technology (EdTech) policies respect children's digital rights. Generative AI is reaching children's education faster than its governance can keep pace, yet checking a tool against children's rights remains manual, expert-dependent, and slow. We propose the Child Rights Impact Score (CRIS), an evidence-linked measure across five dimensions: safety, privacy, transparency, autonomy, and non-discrimination. ChildAI-Gov reads an EdTech tool's privacy or AI policy and scores each dimension by combining a large-language-model judgement (gpt-4o-mini) with a deterministic rule check. A retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) component grounds every score in the governing provisions, retrieved from a curated knowledge base of children's rights frameworks (the EU AI Act, UNICEF guidance, and others), so each score is tied to the evidence behind it and an auditor can trace which provision it rests on. We also construct AIPolicy-EdTech, a dataset of 57 real EdTech policies. On it, the five dimensions cohered as a single measure (Cronbach's alpha = 0.79), and grounding made scoring stricter while preserving rankings; an ungrounded baseline was far more lenient, passing nearly half the policies where ChildAI-Gov passed none. It offers evidence-linked decision support on documented commitments, not observation of real-world behaviour or determinations of legal compliance.

items.title: Neural Defend ARCAS 290M: A Robust Foundation Model for AI-Generated Audio Detection
items.abstract: Voice cloning now needs only seconds of audio, and detectors tuned to one dataset often fail when the generator, channel, or language changes. We introduce ARCAS 290M, Neural Defend's foundation model for detecting AI-generated audio. A single frozen production model, with no benchmark-specific fine-tuning, generalizes across text-to-speech, voice-conversion, and codec-language-model generators, telephone and Bluetooth channels, recording conditions, and languages. We evaluate it on the complete official test sets of ten public benchmarks, scoring every recording exactly as released, and against commercial systems on independent leaderboards. ARCAS 290M ranks first among all systems on the Podonos leaderboard and has the lowest equal error rate among commercial detectors on ASVspoof5. It separates real from AI-generated speech almost perfectly on ASVspoof5, SpeechFake, and ShiftySpeech, and detects nearly all AI-generated speech in Hindi, Tamil, Bengali, and Telugu. On every benchmark with a published zero-shot comparison, including in-the-wild audio, partial fakes, and the conditions hardest for the field, it surpasses the strongest reported detector by a wide margin. These results establish ARCAS 290M as a general-purpose foundation for AI-generated audio detection in fraud prevention, platform safety, and media verification.

items.title: A Benchmark Protocol and Fairness Analysis Towards Open-Set EEG Seizure Type Classification
items.abstract: Automated EEG seizure type classification systems are typically trained and evaluated under the closed-set assumption, where all seizure types encountered at deployment are seen during training. In clinical practice, this assumption fails: patients present with rare or atypical seizure types that fall outside the training label space, and a system that forces a wrong label is worse than one that abstains. We introduce the first open-set recognition protocol for EEG seizure type classification on the Temple University Hospital Seizure Corpus (TUSZ v2.0.3), defining known and unknown classes using the clinical taxonomy itself: seizure types with sufficient subject representation (at least 12 subjects) form the known set, and rare types form the unknown set. We evaluate seven post-hoc open-set scorers (MSP, MaxLogit, energy, Mahalanobis, kNN, GHOST, and COSTARR) applied to a partially fine-tuned EEG Foundation Model (EFM), using a subject-disjoint leave-one-class-out (LOCO) protocol over three seeds that tests whether methods can detect seizure types excluded from fine-tuning. On true unknown classes, the best scorer (Mahalanobis) reaches a mean AUROC of 0.66, and differences among the top scorers are within seed-to-seed variation. Held-out known seizure types from unseen subjects are detected only slightly above chance (AUROC 0.54-0.58 for all scorers). Per-subject rejection rates are highly uneven for all scorers, and GHOST does not significantly improve per-subject fairness over energy scoring (two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank, p >= 0.25). We release the protocol, subject splits, and code as an initial baseline; our results indicate that open-set seizure type recognition remains a hard, open problem.

items.title: Search-RSI: Expanding Search Worlds Along Multimodal Agents' Capability Frontier
items.abstract: Multimodal search agents answer knowledge intensive visual questions by grounding them in retrieved evidence, and recent recipes train them on multi hop tasks that are synthesized from knowledge graphs and grown online to keep pace with the agent. These recipes, however, treat the searchable world as fixed: a new question can be well formed and verifiable while its evidence is absent from the retrieval backend, so the agent issues the right query, retrieves nothing, and is penalized as if its policy were at fault. Such unreachable negatives accumulate with every round of growth. We propose Search-RSI, a recursive self improvement framework that expands the search world along the agent's capability frontier. In each round, the current policy diagnoses its partially mastered regions of a task space spanned by hop depth, relation rarity, and distractor density; new tasks there are grown together with their evidence; and the same policy decides how they are used: candidates on which its probes disagree feed reinforcement learning, while those beyond its reach become hint guided demonstrations of its own. Keeping the policy inside this loop matters: an improver frozen at the start of training loses 3.2 points. On nine multimodal search benchmarks, Search-RSI keeps improving where static task growth saturates, raising the average accuracy of the recipe it builds on by 9.8 and 9.5 points at 9B and 27B, of which 7.0 points are out of reach for a world that is merely made consistent. The loop uses no external model and only privileged task structure that is removed before training, at 1.27x the compute of static growth.

items.title: QuASAR: Toward an LLM-Assisted Framework for Screening, Prototyping, and Assessing Quantum-Advantage Opportunities in Scientific Computing
items.abstract: Identifying scientific computations that could benefit from quantum algorithms requires both domain knowledge and fluency in quantum algorithm design, expertise that rarely resides in one person. We report results from QuASAR, an experimental, two-agent, LLM-driven pipeline intended to bridge this gap. One agent screens scientific literature for computational kernels with a plausible quantum-algorithmic analogue and proposes candidates, each backed by citations. A second agent independently verifies those citations. For candidates that survive verification, it reconstructs the source's computational structure, formulates a quantum mapping, builds and executes a prototype, and benchmarks it against classical baselines. We applied this pipeline to ten candidate computations drawn from the astrophysics literature. Nine candidates were carried through to a small-scale, benchmarked prototype. We report three in detail, chosen as the clearest examples with the least redundancy across the set. They span combinatorial optimization, stochastic simulation, and Bayesian inference. The pipeline attempted to supply quantum-design expertise a domain scientist might lack, reconstructing source algorithms where one existed and building original, disclosed mappings where none did. None of the three case studies achieved quantum advantage at the tested scales, and their astrophysical framing has not yet undergone expert validation. What the experiment does show is that the pipeline can turn a published idea into a runnable prototype, which a scientist can then inspect, test against classical methods, and decide whether to pursue. QuASAR is an exploratory framework, offered to the community for evaluation, critique, and further development, with an approach that could broaden the use of quantum computing in scientific research and extend to computational improvements more generally.

items.title: RoSci: Exploring Robustness in Science VLMs
items.abstract: Recent advancements in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) enable significant progress in scientific tasks. However, these models are generally assumed to be presented with complete and accurate information, overlooking the challenges of erroneous/missing information in wild scenarios. To address this gap, we introduce the concept of Scientific Model Robustness, which defines a model's ability to detect anomalies, assess solvability, and perform self-calibration when faced with Information Error (inconsistencies) or Information Loss (insufficiency). Specifically, we present RoSci-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark of 1,220 samples using a seed-variant strategy across six degradation types. To address VLM fragility, we further propose RoSci-Agent, a framework that employs a Parse-Verify-Decide pipeline to vet premises before reasoning. The evaluated VLMs sometimes answer questions whose premises are invalid or incomplete. RoSci-Agent achieves a higher Overall Robustness Score than the evaluated standalone VLMs. RoSci-Bench gives the multimodal reasoning community a common test of when models answer, request clarification, or reject a scientific question.

items.title: Shared Understanding in Human-AI Teams: Coordination Continuity in Evolving Work
items.abstract: People are increasingly working with AI agents as part of extended, asynchronous workflows. In these settings, shared access to information does not guarantee a shared basis for action: goals, plans, and roles may persist while their current significance changes. We introduce coordination continuity, the extent to which collaborators sustain a workable basis for interdependent action as work progresses. Drawing on research on collaborative work, along with two qualitative team studies and a reflexive case from our own repository-based environment, we present a framework of three elements: durable representations of collaborative work; relative coordination properties that support interpretation of representations in the moment; and interaction mechanisms through which the status of representations can be understood and altered. We use a build-act-drift-rebuild heuristic and the notion of consequential moments to characterise when rebuilding may be needed. We draw eight design implications for collaborative AI infrastructure.
