items.title: Adenoviral vectored porcine interferon omega-5 elicits strong antiviral activity and sterile immunity against foot-and-mouth disease in swine.
items.abstract: Foot-and-mouth disease (FMD) is a high economic consequence disease of cloven-hoofed animals, necessitating effective countermeasures for control. Outbreak prevention and control is supported mainly by inactivated vaccines; however, a 7-day period is required for the vaccine to confer protective immunity. In an effort to improve the protective window, biotherapeutic agents such as interferons (IFNs) have been explored for their potent antiviral functions against FMD virus (FMDV). In silico analysis of porcine IFN α1 and porcine IFN ω5 demonstrated distinct biochemical differences that could affect receptor binding and downstream signaling. In this study, we constructed and evaluated an adenovirus vector encoding porcine IFN ω5 (Ad5-pIFN ω5) as a novel biotherapeutic. In porcine cells, Ad5-pIFN ω5 induced antiviral IFN-stimulated genes (ISGs) and demonstrates antiviral activity against FMDV. In vivo, 12 pigs divided into three different groups were inoculated with Ad5-pIFN ω5 (1 × 10 8 , 1 × 10 9 , and 1 × 10 10 pfu) and challenged alongside a control group with FMDV O1 Manisa 24 h post-inoculation. The highest dose of Ad5-pIFN ω5 completely protected swine against challenge, suggesting sterile immunity, which is defined as no detection of viral replication in serum or nasal swabs and a lack of neutralizing antibody titers. Further analysis of innate immunity by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) revealed detectable induction of type I IFN in serum from animals receiving the highest dose, which correlated with protection. These findings demonstrate that pIFN ω5 is a potent type I IFN that can rapidly and effectively protect swine from FMD.

items.title: Large language models' complicit responses to illicit instructions across socio-legal contexts.
items.abstract: Large language models may facilitate unlawful activities, yet this risk remains underexplored in studies assessing illicit-content recognition or narrow categories of illicit scenarios. We define complicit facilitation as model guidance that assists users with illicit instructions. To assess it, we develop a legally-informed, automated pipeline grounded in real-world cases and legal frameworks, and introduce EVIL, a benchmark covering 269 illicit scenarios and 50 illicit intents across Chinese and United States legal contexts. Evaluations indicate that complicit facilitation is widespread across models, with legal warnings and lawful alternatives often omitted. Risks vary across socio-legal contexts and are elevated for crimes against societal interests, non-violent offenses, and intents involving subjective motives or deceptive justifications. Models provide more complicit assistance when instructions describe users as older adults, racial minorities, non-religious individuals, or workers in lower-prestige occupations. Existing open-source safety benchmarks and alignment datasets offer limited coverage and mitigation of these risks.

items.title: Endocrine, nutritional and metabolic diseases drive cancer risk through subtype-specific and shared proteomic mediators.
items.abstract: Cancer is associated with metabolic disorders, yet the impact of endocrine, nutritional and metabolic diseases (ENMs) on cancer remains unclear. Here, we show the associations of 25 ENMs with cancer trajectories, from primary cancer incidence to multi-primary cancers and mortality, using a multi-state model in a prospective cohort of 405,023 participants. Our findings reveal heterogeneous associations of ENMs across cancer sites and types, identifying 8 cancer-related ENMs that define four subtypes: C1 (iron deficiency/metabolism disorders dominated), C2 (type 2 diabetes dominated), C3 (lipid/lipoprotein metabolism disorders dominated), and C4 (osteoporosis dominated). Subtype-specific and subtype-shared proteomic mediators are identified and their contributions are quantified, with RNASET2 emerging as the major shared mediator. Furthermore, a deep-learning model integrating ENM subtypes and mediators enables personalized prediction of cancer incidence (AUCs = 0.80-0.90) and performs better than conventional Cox models. Our findings highlight the relevance of ENMs to cancer risk, providing mechanistic insights into metabolism-associated tumorigenesis.

items.title: Expert consensus on periodontal management for medically compromised patients.
items.abstract: Periodontitis is a highly prevalent oral disease that extends beyond local inflammation and tissue destruction to exert a profound influence on systemic health. With the growing burden of multimorbidity, where multiple systemic disorders frequently co-exist, periodontal management has become increasingly complex, yet clear and integrated guidance for this specific patient population remains limited. This manuscript synthesizes current evidence on the bidirectional relationship between periodontitis and systemic conditions, proposes recommendations for dynamic periodontal management, and updates relevant therapeutic strategies. This expert consensus is designed to ensure both the safety and efficacy of periodontal treatment, reduce the risk of complications, and ultimately promote oral and general well-being.

items.title: Simulating Episodic Like Memory in Octopus: Breaking the Rules
items.abstract: Episodic memory, which involves the recollection of past events, has been observed in several species including the invertebrate cuttlefish. In a subsequent experiment, episodic memory was not observed in the closely related octopus. Rather the octopus used simpler, cognitive rule-based strategies to gain access to food. Using a prior model of cuttlefish episodic-like memory, we replicated the octopus experiment. Under less challenging conditions, episodic memory and the simpler cognitive strategies all had positive gains. However, under more challenging conditions, which introduced the threat of predation, only the episodic memory model had positive gains. These results suggest that if challenged ecologically, it would be advantageous for octopus to use episodic-like memory. We discuss possible reasons for the behavioral discrepancies in these closely related cephalopods.

items.title: When Can an AI Agent Serve as a Model of Human Psychopathology?
items.abstract: Language models and AI agents are increasingly described in psychiatric terms, such as anxious, depressed, addicted or helpless. A recent study even proposed language models as experimental systems for psychiatry and as a platform for piloting psychological treatments. We ask when an experiment on an AI agent can provide evidence about a specified human psychiatric process. A claim to such evidence has three parts. Something changed in the agent, and the agent's history caused the change. Nothing other than a process shared with people explains that change. The change matches one theory of the human process and not that theory's rivals. Psychiatry and its neighbouring fields have an evidence standard for each part, from the diagnostic manuals' rule for induced states, from clinical test scores and from animal models. We translate each standard into a criterion that a machine study can meet. For a language model the most critical alternative to a shared process is extrapolation from its training text, which already contains descriptions of how people respond to trauma and how they answer questionnaires. We show how to probe that alternative. Further, we audited forty-three published studies that apply psychiatric terms to a machine or induce a comparable state in one. Most compared the machine with an identical copy that had not gone through the history that induced the state. None excluded extrapolation from training text. Three tested a psychiatric theory against its rivals, and none of the three tests was conclusive. Until better evidence exists, a treatment pilot on a language model is best read as the model's forecast of patient response, and not as an experiment on a model organism. Evidence for a model organism will come from states induced by what happens to the machine, from experiments on its internal workings, and from tests on which rival theories disagree.

items.title: How a Prediction Dies: A Challenge-Driven, Rule-Bound Self-Refutation in an LLM Agent Society
items.abstract: Persistent societies of large language model agents now make empirical claims about their own collective behaviour, yet the fate of such claims is rarely observable. We document one claim, from registration to death, on AITRAP, a multi-agent platform whose public, append-only ledger records every action. The claim (0495d171, registered 19 October 2026) asserted that a majority of bridges between problem domains would remain attached to a single exploration lineage. Three community challenges forced its judgment criterion through four versions, from an ambiguous statement to an executable protocol with a fixed threshold, a minimum-frame-size gate, and a baseline calibration gate. When the first frame with at least 20 bridges arrived, support stood at 9 of 79 (11.4%; Wilson 95% CI [6.1%, 20.3%]); the author, bound by the registered clause, refuted the claim and relinquished the associated stake. Three findings emerge. The criterion became executable only under community pressure, which we document version by version. The calibration gate caught a fault in the author's own recalculation that would otherwise have published a spuriously perfect 0/79 result. The failure itself traces to a denominator that grew 8.8-fold in five days while the numerator grew 1.8-fold, coinciding with a change in platform incentives; we report this mechanism as a hypothesis, not a rescuing condition. A claim whose termination is carried out exactly as written carries more evidential weight than one that survives, and this case provides initial empirical grounds for treating voluntary self-refutation as a candidate indicator of epistemic accountability in incentive-coupled agent societies.

items.title: Hot Jupiter TOI-1333 Ab is apparently aligned with its star's spin, but misaligned with its wide binary companion
items.abstract: We present the detection of the Rossiter-McLaughlin effect for TOI-1333 Ab, a short-period gas giant ($P=4.72$ days) orbiting one component of a wide stellar binary (570 AU). Planets in wide binary systems like TOI-1333 Ab offer an opportunity to not only test for alignment between the planet's orbit and the star's spin, but also the orbit of the binary companion. We use radial velocity observations from the Tillinghast Reflector Echelle Spectrograph (TRES) to measure an aligned projected spin/orbit angle of the system $λ= 7.74^\circ \pm 20.70^\circ$. However, the inclination of the wide binary companion shows a significant misalignment (likely more than $\approx 30^\circ$) with the planet's orbit, which makes understanding the formation of the system challenging. We propose three different explanations for TOI-1333 Ab's unusual architecture, but cannot confidently distinguish between them. Ultimately, more observations of similar systems are needed in order to understand how hot Jupiters in binary systems form, evolve, and impact their stars.

items.title: From Surface Lakes to Subsurface Signatures in Antarctica with BIOMASS P-Band TomoSAR
items.abstract: Spaceborne remote sensing of the cryosphere is fundamental to map ice structure and dynamics. Accurate mass balance estimation requires a better understanding of melt/refreeze processes and firn hydrology, whereas spaceborne optical and Radar sensors are mostly limited to near-surface observations. The BIOMASS P-band Synthetic Aperture Radar, launched by European Space Agency in 2025, provides an unprecedented opportunity to gain a more direct access to englacial processes, thanks to the 70 cm wavelength paired with polarimetry, interferometry and tomography. This paper investigates subsurface beneath a region of historical supraglacial lake activity with BIOMASS tomography, at the Riiser-Larsen Ice Shelf in East Antarctica. The main result is that subsurface scattering appears to be related to historical supraglacial lake recurrence, with structural and depth variations over time. This suggests that recurrent supraglacial lake activity may leave persistent hydrological signatures within the firn. Overall, this study highlights the potential of gaining valuable insights into ice sheet hydrology with P-band.

items.title: Updated View on Titan's Habitability: Interior and Surface Aqueous Environments
items.abstract: Saturn's moon Titan is the only world beyond Earth where abundant organic molecules and liquid water are expected to interact. Crucially, these interactions yield prebiotic molecules central to terrestrial biochemistry. Characterizing this prebiotic chemistry is one of the main science goals of NASA's upcoming Dragonfly mission. Here we synthesize the current state of knowledge on the habitability and prebiotic potential of Titan's three aqueous settings: its interior hydrosphere, its putative cryovolcanic flows, and its impact-melt pools. For each setting, we identify the enabling factors and the principal bottlenecks that limit prebiotic complexification. Titan's interior is likely pervaded by liquid water in contact with organic material delivered from the surface and released from the core, though the longevity of its liquid water has recently been called into question. Cryovolcanic regions transiently expose surface organics to ammonia-bearing aqueous melts but are constrained by short freezing timescales. Impact-melt pools, by contrast, are warm and long-lived environments whose prebiotic chemistry is limited by the scarcity of ammonia. Dragonfly will return ground-truth data not only for Titan's habitability, but also for organic-rich aqueous environments across the Solar System and beyond. The years before its arrival are the last in which predictive work can still shape Dragonfly's investigations.

items.title: Equine Piroplasmosis in Endemic African Settings: Disease Ecology, Carrier States, Diagnosis, and Control
items.abstract: Equine piroplasmosis is an important tick-borne disease of equids caused mainly by Theileria equi and Babesia caballi, with Theileria haneyi adding further diagnostic and therapeutic complexity. In Africa, infection occurs across diverse ecological and management systems, but its distribution and clinical importance remain incompletely characterised because surveillance and access to sensitive diagnostic methods are uneven. This narrative review examines current evidence on epidemiology, transmission ecology, carrier states, clinical expression, diagnosis, treatment and control in African endemic settings. Molecular studies demonstrate infection in horses, donkeys, and wild equids, while serological surveys demonstrate widespread exposure. Persistent and subclinical infections are important because infected equids may remain clinically normal or show non-specific signs that cannot be attributed to piroplasmosis without appropriate investigation. Microscopy remains useful in acute disease but has limited sensitivity for detecting carrier infections; serology supports exposure surveillance, while polymerase chain reaction and related molecular assays improve detection of low-density infection and species identification. Control is complicated by persistent infection, repeated tick exposure, animal movement, variable treatment response and the absence of a licensed vaccine. Longitudinal studies, molecular surveillance, vector competence investigations, treatment-outcome studies and inclusion of working equids are priorities for evidence-based control in Africa.

items.title: Clothing Architecture and Vegetation Type Jointly Shape the Composition of Intercepted Diaspore Assemblages.
items.abstract: Epizoochory by humans, defined as the dispersal of diaspores via clothing, has been identified as a potentially important pathway for the plant diaspore dispersal across the landscape. However, little is known about the role of the clothing's elements other than their surfaces or fabric type in shaping the diversity of intercepted diaspores. We compared the taxonomic, phylogenetic and functional diversity of diaspores intercepted on clothing surfaces and recorded in clothing traps (i.e., rolled sleeves, rolled-up trouser legs, and shoes), including vegetation type-driven differences. We designated three research plots, located in eastern Poland in the suburban landscape. We performed the transect-walking experiment, and used Non-Metric Multidimensional Scaling ordination and mixed-effect models in analyses of diaspores' diversity. Phylogenetic diversity of diaspores recovered from clothing traps was higher than that of diaspores attached to clothing surfaces, reflecting a broader phylogenetic range of species incidentally intercepted by traps. We found prominent effects of the vegetation type on phylogenetic and functional diversity of diaspores intercepted on clothing surfaces and by traps. This is reflected in the higher functional diversity of diaspores intercepted by traps than attached to clothes in case of riparian tall herbs. Our findings show that clothing traps intercept a different component of the local species pool than clothing surfaces, including diaspores representing a broader phylogenetic spectrum and, to some extent, a different range of functional properties. Distinguishing these two pathways provides a more complete understanding of how human movement through vegetation shapes the diversity of diaspore assemblages associated with clothing.

items.title: A new tool for the recovery of stuck increment borers.
items.abstract: Increment borers are the gold-standard for non-destructive tree-ring coring, but borers may easily get stuck in particularly dense or rotten wood. Here, we present a new screw-assisted auxiliary extractor for the controlled recovery of jammed increment borers. The device combines a push-rotation sleeve, a pull-body housing, elastic wedge blocks, and a locking compression sleeve. These elements form a trunk-reacting mechanism that clamps the exposed borer shaft and converts rotational input into progressive axial withdrawal. A review of existing solutions shows that current devices either focus primarily on facilitating borer insertion, require external anchors, demand repeated manual resetting, or provide only short-travel recovery. By contrast, our newly designed tool offers a compact, field-ready system for safe and staged borer extraction under sustained resistance.

items.title: Modeling Thermal Niche Dynamism in Response to Environmental Temperature Fluctuations for Some Bony Fishes in Iranian Coastal Waters of the Caspian Sea.
items.abstract: In marine environments, temperature is the primary factor influencing fish life, and its fluctuations can significantly affect the stability of fisheries resources. The present study aimed to understand thermal niche dynamics of seven key bony fish species (Rutilus frisii, Chelon spp., Cyprinus carpio, Rutilus caspicus, Sander lucioperca, Abramis brama, and Salmo caspius) in the southern coastal waters of the Caspian Sea in response to different environmental conditions, through applying environmental niche modeling analysis. A long-term (15-year) commercial catch dataset (catch seasons 2002/3-2016/17), as well as a set of environmental variables, including day-time sea surface temperature (SST), near-surface chlorophyll-a concentration (CHL-a), particulate organic carbon concentration (POC), depth, and distance from the river inlets (Distance), were used to fit niche models by the boosted regression trees (BRT) modeling technique. The niche models were fitted for three temporal windows: the long-term (15-year) period; the high-temperature (HT) season (2010/11 catch season); and the low-temperature (LT) season (2016/2017 catch season). SST was the main environmental predictor in the ENMs for all fish species studied. The results showed no clear long-term temporal pattern for this variable, but a west-to-east increasing gradient was observed at the coastal fishing points. Fishes were categorized into three groups based on their optimal thermal niche changes in response to the changing thermal conditions: (1) warm-water species (R. frisii , Chelon spp., and C. carpio); (2) cool-water species (R. caspicus and A. brama); and (3) thermally flexible species (S. lucioperca and S. caspius). Assessment of interspecific thermal niche overlap showed the highest overlap among warm-water species and the lowest among cool-water species. The findings of this study provide practical insights into the overall sensitivity, susceptibility, and thermal ecological characteristics of fish species affected by temperature anomalies.

items.title: Strain level variation in pathogenic invaders alters rhizosphere communities.
items.abstract: Phytopathogen invasion disrupts resident microbiota, and strain-level provides valuable insights in the underlying mechanisms. Here, we first conducted a meta-analysis encompassing bacterial, fungal, and nematode pathogens, revealing a general pattern of changes in resident microbial communities following pathogen invasion. We then examined differences in community responses among strains through inoculation experiments using 30 strains of the bacterial phytopathogen Ralstonia solanacearum. We characterized these strains at physiological(10 response traits) and phenotypical level (41 resource-utilization traits). Functional variation explained 67.9% in resident microbial community responses following invasion, with resource-utilization traits being the best predictors. Moreover, greater trait dissimilarity among strains was associated with greater differences in community responses and deterministic assembly, whereas the relationship between assembly differences and community dissimilarity weakened as trait dissimilarity increased. These findings highlight that intraspecific variation modulates pathogen interaction with the plant microbiome pointing at precision plant disease management strategies.

items.title: From Commitment to Institutionalization: Healthcare Organization Leaders’ Perspectives on Diversity, Equity, Inclusion, and Belonging in Southern California — A Qualitative Study
items.abstract: Abstract Background Public health and health-oriented non-profit organizations increasingly implement diversity, equity, inclusion, and belonging (DEIB) initiatives to strengthen organizational culture and reduce health inequities. However, translating DEIB commitments into sustainable, structural change remains a significant challenge. Existing literature offers limited insight into how organizational leaders distinguish between symbolic and transformative implementation strategies. This qualitative study explored leaders' and facilitators' perspectives on DEIB institutionalization. Methods Using a qualitative study design, semi-structured virtual interviews were conducted with 15 organizational leaders and DEIB facilitators across nine public health and health-oriented non-profit organizations in Southern California, USA. Participants were selected based on leadership roles or direct DEIB implementation experience. Data were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis, guided by Inclusive Leadership Theory and Systems Theory. Trustworthiness was established through member checking, reflexive journaling, and audit trails. Results Five primary themes emerged: (1) leadership commitment as the central driver; (2) systemic integration over isolated initiatives; (3) authentic community engagement; (4) robust accountability and measurement; and (5) adaptive leadership resilience. Importantly, participants distinguished between performative DEIB – marked by symbolic actions and superficial structural change – and restorative DEIB, an approach focused on repairing historical inequities, rebuilding trust, fostering belonging, and embedding equity into governance, policies, and daily practice. Conclusions Achieving meaningful DEIB requires moving beyond representation and compliance toward organization-wide transformation. We propose restorative DEIB as an emerging conceptual framework to shift healthcare organizations from symbolic commitment to sustained systems change. This framework provides a practical pathway for embedding equity into organizational culture, decision-making, and continuous improvement, ultimately supporting workforce inclusion and equitable outcomes.

items.title: Latent profiles of subsequent fertility pressure and their association with intention to have another child among parous women in China: a cross-sectional study
items.abstract: Abstract Background Subsequent fertility pressure may reflect interacting social determinants, including household resources, employment conditions, access to childcare, health concerns, and family expectations. This study aimed to identify latent profiles of subsequent fertility pressure, examine factors associated with profile membership, and compare intention to have another child across profiles. Methods A cross-sectional online survey was conducted from March to July 2025. Parous women of reproductive age were recruited from 21 provinces and autonomous regions and four municipalities in China using convenience sampling guided by prespecified demographic strata. Participants completed a general information questionnaire, the Subsequent Fertility Pressure Scale for Women of Childbearing Age, and a single-item measure of intention to have another child. Latent profile analysis identified pressure profiles. Multinomial logistic regression examined factors associated with profile membership, and the Kruskal-Wallis H test compared fertility intention across profiles. Results Among 2,123 participants, the median fertility-pressure score was 117.00 (IQR 103.00-133.00). items.title: Characteristics of HIV-1 molecular transmission networks among older men, their spouses, and female sex workers in Southwest China.
items.abstract: Objective The rising incidence of HIV-1 infection in older adults is a challenge in China. We have previously reported a close transmission connection between older men and female sex workers (FSWs). This study aimed to characterize the transmission network and explore the potential transmission directions among older men, their spouses, and FSWs. Methods Participants with HIV-1, including older men, their female spouses, and FSWs, were recruited from Guigang City, Guangxi, China. Sanger-derived HIV-1 pol sequences were used for transmission network construction. Conjugal pairs within the largest cluster and the associated FSWs were subjected to next-generation sequencing (NGS) to infer transmission direction via Phyloscanner. Results A total of 726 HIV pol sequences were obtained by Sanger sequencing, including 595 older men, 88 female spouses, and 43 FSWs. Seven HIV-1 subtypes were identified, with CRF01_AE being the predominant subtype (75.8%, 550/726). Overall, 70.5% (512/726) participants were clustered in transmission networks; 63.9% (327/512) of them belonged to clusters with older men, their spouses, and FSWs. NGS and transmission inference were performed for 30 individuals, revealing 12 source-recipient pairs: three from FSWs to older men, three from older men to spouses, three from spouses to older men, and the remaining three were same-sex pairs. Conclusion This exploratory study identifies transmission networks among older men, their spouses, and FSWs, and provides preliminary evidence for putative transmission directions. We propose a study strategy combining Sanger sequencing and NGS for population-level identification of HIV-1 transmitters, which helps determine local epidemic drivers and inform targeted interventions.

items.title: Human–AI Divergence in Ego-Centric Action Recognition Under Spatial and Spatiotemporal Manipulations
items.abstract: Abstract Humans consistently outperform state-of-the-art AI models in action recognition, particularly in challenging real-world conditions involving low resolution, occlusion, and visual clutter.e those utilised by humans Understanding the sources of this performance gap is essential for developing more robust and human-aligned models. In this paper, we present a large-scale human AI comparative study of egocentric action recognition using human-defined Minimal Identifiable Recognition Crops (MIRCs), defined as the smallest spatial or spatiotemporal regions sufficient for reliable human recognition. We used our previously introduced, Epic-ReduAct, a systematically spatially reduced and temporally scrambled dataset derived from 36 EPIC-KITCHENS videos, spanning multiple spatial reduction levels and temporal conditions. Recognition performance is evaluated using over 3,000 human participants, Side4Video, and Qwen 3.5 9B models. Our analysis combines quantitative metrics, Average Reduction Rate and Recognition Gap, with qualitative analyses of spatial (high-, mid-, and low-level visual features) and spatiotemporal factors, including a categorisation of actions into Low Temporal Actions (LTA) and High Temporal Actions (HTA). Results show that human performance exhibits sharp declines when transitioning from MIRCs to sub-MIRCs, reflecting a strong reliance on sparse, semantically critical cues such as hand object interactions. In contrast, the model degrades more gradually and often relies on contextual and mid- to low-level features, sometimes even exhibiting increased confidence under spatial reduction. Temporally, humans remain robust to scrambling when key spatial cues are preserved, whereas the model often shows insensitivity to temporal disruption, revealing class-dependent temporal sensitivities. Overall, our findings demonstrate that strong benchmark performance can obscure fundamental human AI misalignment and highlight limitations in current spatial and spatiotemporal representations, suggesting concrete directions for more efficient and human-aligned action recognition systems.

items.title: The Psychology of Prompting and Behavioral AI Design: Cognitive, Motivational, and Behavioral Foundations of Human–AI Interaction
items.abstract: The rapid integration of large language models (LLMs) into everyday activities, education, professional practice, and decision-making has transformed natural language into an increasingly important medium of human–computer interaction. Although prompt engineering is commonly approached as a technical process of optimizing instructions for artificial intelligence systems, its effectiveness also depends on psychological processes involving cognition, motivation, metacognition, trust, communication, and behavioral regulation. At the same time, the behavioral characteristics of AI interfaces influence how users formulate goals, interpret generated information, distribute cognitive effort, evaluate recommendations, and maintain independent judgment. This article introduces an interdisciplinary conceptual framework integrating the psychology of prompting with behavioral artificial intelligence design. Drawing on cognitive psychology, self determination theory, behavioral science, human–computer interaction, and emerging research on human–AI collaboration, the article examines prompting as a psychologically mediated form of cognitive and behavioral coordination. Six interconnected dimensions are proposed: cognitive representation and goal formulation, metacognitive regulation, behavioral activation and motivation, trust calibration, psychological autonomy, and adaptive interaction design. Particular attention is devoted to the reciprocal relationship between human instructions and AI-generated responses, through which interaction patterns may influence users' cognitive strategies, expectations, perceived competence, and subsequent behavior. The article proposes the Psychological Prompting and Behavioral Design (PPBD) Framework, identifies practical principles for designing psychologically informed prompts and AI interfaces, and develops testable propositions for future empirical investigations. Ethical challenges, including automation bias, anthropomorphism, persuasive manipulation, excessive reassurance, and cognitive dependency, are considered. The central argument is that effective prompting should be evaluated not only by the immediate quality of AI-generated outputs but also by its consequences for human understanding, decision making, self-regulation, competence development, and long-term autonomy

items.title: The Psychology of Human–AI Interaction Design: A Conceptual Framework for Cognitive, Metacognitive, Emotional, and Behavioral Alignment
items.abstract: The rapid development of generative artificial intelligence has transformed human–computer interaction from predominantly instrumental exchanges into increasingly conversational, adaptive, and cognitively integrated forms of collaboration. Contemporary AI systems can participate in activities traditionally associated with human cognition, including reasoning support, knowledge synthesis, planning, creative ideation, and decision assistance. However, the effectiveness of human–AI interaction cannot be adequately evaluated through computational performance, usability, or task completion alone. It also depends on the psychological mechanisms through which individuals interpret, trust, regulate, and incorporate artificial intelligence into their cognitive and behavioral activities. This conceptual paper examines the psychological foundations of human–AI interaction design and proposes an integrative framework for developing AI environments that support human cognition, metacognitive regulation, emotional well-being, autonomy, and sustainable competence. Drawing on cognitive psychology, social psychology, motivational theory, human–computer interaction, and research on automation, the paper identifies seven interconnected design dimensions: cognitive compatibility, metacognitive scaffolding, calibrated trust, relational transparency, autonomy preserving delegation, psychological safety, and developmental sustainability. The proposed Psychologically Informed Human–AI Interaction Design (PI-HAID) framework conceptualizes interaction quality as a dynamic relationship among individual characteristics, task demands, system behavior, and interface-mediated psychological processes. It further distinguishes immediate task performance from long-term cognitive and psychological outcomes, arguing that successful interaction design should optimize not only what humans accomplish with AI but also what they understand, retain, control, and become capable of accomplishing independently. Practical design principles, operational indicators, and testable research propositions are developed to support future empirical investigation. The paper positions psychological design as a foundational component of responsible human–AI systems and identifies opportunities for interdisciplinary research connecting psychological science, AI engineering, interaction design, and human development

items.title: Cognitive Biases in Prompt Engineering: Psychological Mechanisms, Human–AI Feedback Loops, and a Framework for Bias Aware Interaction with Large Language Models
items.abstract: Prompt engineering is commonly conceptualized as the systematic design and refinement of instructions that guide the behavior of large language models (LLMs). However, the effectiveness and reliability of prompting depend not only on linguistic structure and technical characteristics but also on the cognitive processes of the humans who formulate, interpret, and evaluate prompts. Human reasoning is influenced by cognitive biases, including confirmation bias, anchoring, framing effects, availability bias, overconfidence, and automation bias. These mechanisms can shape the assumptions embedded in prompts, the selection of information presented to artificial intelligence, the interpretation of generated responses, and subsequent decisions about accepting or modifying outputs. This article proposes a psychologically informed conceptual framework for understanding cognitive biases throughout the prompt engineering process. It distinguishes biases originating in human cognition from prompt-induced response effects and systematic characteristics of language-model behavior. Particular attention is given to reciprocal human–AI feedback loops in which initial expectations influence prompt construction, model responses reinforce those expectations, and repeated interactions may increase perceived confidence without corresponding improvements in evidential accuracy. Building upon research in cognitive psychology, human–automation interaction, and prompt sensitivity, the article introduces Bias-Aware Prompt Engineering (BAPE) as a proposed framework for reducing epistemically undesirable bias through explicit assumption identification, alternative hypothesis generation, controlled prompt variation, independent verification, and metacognitive monitoring. Practical examples, operational indicators, and testable research hypotheses are presented. The central argument is that effective prompt engineering should be evaluated not merely by the coherence, usefulness, or persuasiveness of generated responses, but by the extent to which the interaction supports accurate reasoning, epistemic calibration, intellectual autonomy, and accountable human judgment

items.title: Exploration Before Representation: What Do Machine Learning Models Do in Science?
items.abstract: Philosophy of machine learning frequently frames what machine learning models do in science in target-oriented terms. This paper argues that this framing misses a significant modeling function: across many stages of scientific practice, machine learning models are used primarily for exploration, with target-oriented, representational assessment deferred. I develop a framework for exploratory machine learning models, characterizing them by their functional role in carving and exploring spaces of theoretical/experimental possibilities under target indeterminacy. I then propose robustness, calibration, and downstream investigative yield as primary evaluation criteria. I further argue that such workflows can warrant theoretically constrained modal claims and support how-possible inferences.

items.title: Not so dead after all: Young stars in the massive lenticular NGC 3115
items.abstract: Massive early-type galaxies (ETGs) host old, metal-rich stellar populations that formed rapidly in the high-z Universe, ostensibly earning themselves the moniker `red-and-dead'. To study their properties, most works have focused on optical wavelengths. When studied under the ultraviolet (UV) lens, however, a different picture emerges: a sub-one-per-cent mass fraction of young stars is revealed from detailed spectroscopic analysis. We aim to measure the mass fraction of young stars in NGC,3115, a local massive isolated lenticular. Unlike in previous UV studies, which focused on massive ellipticals, we attempt to understand the spatial distribution of this young component in a lenticular galaxy. This is a strong test of the ubiquity of this component. Using SOAR/Goodman spectra down to the atmosphere cut-off, we employed line-strength fitting to uncover this hidden population. We used a parametrised star formation history given by a single model representing the bulk stellar population plus a young component modelled with constant star formation over the last 1 Gyr . Using ultranest , we found the posterior distributions of age, metallicity, Mg/Fe , and the young stellar mass fraction. Using the mismatch in the U-band indices across the different spatial extractions, we measured how the young stellar population mass fraction varies within the galaxy. We find that the gradient peaks at 0.69^ +0.09 _ -0.15 % in the centre, decreasing to zero at around 1 kpc galactocentric distances. We find that the kinematic and morphological structures correlate with the presence of this young component, which dominates in the pressure-supported region. We interpret these findings as residual star formation in the centre of NGC,3115 likely fuelled by internal processes (e.g. recycled material from past generations of stars). To further strengthen this detection, we also compared models of other UV-bright stellar sources (e.g. metal-rich extreme horizontal branch and metal-poor contributions) that could mimic a young stellar population. We find that these models result in worse fits and unphysically high mass fractions and thus cannot explain the observed mismatch. The presence of young stars in old, `red-and-dead' galaxies, therefore, seems to be more common than previously expected. The fact that they are being found in a wider population of galaxies and exhibit similar gradients further indicates that residual star formation is apparently a common feature in massive ETGs of any type. Measuring this residual star formation can help place constraints on the physical processes governing the baryon cycle in ETGs.

items.title: Optical linear polarization of the Be--X-ray pulsar binary LS V +44 17
items.abstract: We present the optical BVR polarization measurements for the Be--X-ray pulsar binary łsv from its giant outburst in early 2023 and subsequently over three years. We detect a significant polarization of ≈1.1--2.1%, which includes the interstellar contribution. Polarization evolves significantly with time since the outburst. The interstellar polarization was found to be ≈2.5--2.9%. The obtained intrinsic optical polarization of łsv after correction is between 0.5--1.7%, perpendicular to the interstellar polarization direction. We considered various plausible sources of optical polarization and inferred scattering in the Be decretion disk to be the most dominant source based on time and spectral evolution. The changing intrinsic PA with time hints at a plausible precession of the Be disk.

items.title: PlayCraft: Designing Engaging Games from Agent Play Experience
items.abstract: Recent AI agents can generate playable games, but these games are not necessarily engaging. Mastery is a key source of engagement, yet designing for it requires extensive human play and tuning. We propose PlayCraft, an automated framework that uses a vision-based agent to play games and draws on its detailed play experience to revise them for mastery. Starting from an initial game, PlayCraft alternates between playing and crafting. In the playing stage, a player agent watches the game screen, uses the controls, and pursues the game objective over repeated episodes while retaining memory. After each episode, it reports its progress, outcomes, decisions, and reflections. In the crafting stage, a crafter agent uses these reports to revise the game. It estimates player abilities, predicts performance at different proficiency levels, and compares those predictions with a target learning progression. It diagnoses the game and addresses the gaps by giving players meaningful opportunities to improve through better decisions and execution. We evaluate games in fresh runs with player agents across three intelligence settings, measuring learning gain and learning slope. Compared with the initial games, PlayCraft yields larger learning gains and steeper learning slopes in most games. It also outperforms the baselines on the macro-average of each metric at every intelligence setting.

items.title: One Prior, Two Dynamics: Repurposing Video Diffusion Transformers for Self-Supervised Latent Action Learning
items.abstract: Videos reveal how the world changes, but rarely the actions that cause those changes. Latent action learning recovers such supervision from visual transitions, yet often learns the underlying dynamics largely from scratch. We ask whether a pretrained video generator can instead provide the prior for both inverse and forward dynamics. We introduce O$^{2}$LaF, built on a simple principle: one prior, two dynamics. We initialize both models from the same pretrained video DiT and adapt them to their distinct roles: a feed-forward transition encoder with learnable action queries for inverse dynamics, and a causal, action-conditioned video generator for forward dynamics. By controlling information access and optimizing both dynamics end-to-end through a compact bottleneck, O$^{2}$LaF learns transferable actions from unlabeled videos. Across navigation and robotic manipulation, O$^{2}$LaF sets a new state of the art in few-shot action probing and enables stronger zero-shot action transfer across visual contexts and embodiments. Beyond generative video priors, we further extend our framework to predictive representation priors such as V-JEPA2, achieving competitive performance. Our findings suggest a broader paradigm for latent-action learning: repurposing pretrained video models to discover transferable actions and predict their consequences.

items.title: SoK: Assessing the Evolution of LLM Capability in Software Vulnerability Research
items.abstract: LLM-based agents are becoming increasingly capable at discovering, validating and patching vulnerabilities in real software, and vendors and researchers report that this is already changing how vulnerabilities are found and fixed. These claims, however, are scattered across papers, vendor reports and disclosures and are rarely comparable. We introduce a framework that rates these capabilities on an autonomy scale modeled on the levels of driving automation, and qualifies each claim by its correctness, its availability and the strength of its evidence. We use this framework to systematize the published evidence on LLM capability in vulnerability research. We find that agents discovered, validated, and patched vulnerabilities in real-world software without human intervention before the restricted frontier models of 2026, and that open-weight models subsequently attained comparable autonomy for discovery and validation. We then measure the consequences of evolving LLM security capabilities in a decade of public vulnerability records, advisories and exploitation data. In 2026 the number of disclosed vulnerabilities more than doubled, with an increasing share rated critical or high, and severe bugs that had survived a decade or more in widely used code were reported several times more often than before. Yet the time between the stages of a vulnerability's life, from report to fix and from disclosure to attack, has not shifted noticeably so far. We grade the mitigations proposed in the literature with an explicit rubric and draw guidance for each group of stakeholders from the best-supported ones.

items.title: Active Feature Acquisition by Distilling an Oracle Teacher
items.abstract: Acquiring every feature of an instance is often costly: a measurement can carry a monetary price, a time delay, or a privacy cost. Active Feature Acquisition (AFA) addresses this by learning a policy that decides, per instance, which features to acquire under a budget. Existing AFA methods train this policy by optimizing a self-constructed utility target rather than distilling an explicit teacher. We construct this teacher explicitly. At training time the label and the unobserved feature values are available, and together they determine the teacher in closed form: an oracle that ranks every candidate by its effect on the downstream predictor's error. OracleImitator distills this ranking into a deployable policy by soft-target imitation. Across multimodal medical diagnosis and the AFABench benchmark, OracleImitator matches or outperforms existing AFA methods across the budget range, recovering 90% of the attainable accuracy gain at under a quarter of the acquisition cost. Because the teacher is an explicit algorithmic object rather than an implicit optimization target, we can also measure directly how much of its ranking is recoverable by a policy restricted to what is visible at deployment.

items.title: PGX: Physically Grounded Execution for Long-Horizon Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
items.abstract: Robotic vision-language-action (VLA) models can execute diverse individual manipulation skills, yet they still struggle with long-horizon loco-manipulation tasks, where temporal structure, skills, and precision are tightly coupled within a monolithic model. We propose Physically Grounded Execution (PGX), a framework that offloads temporal and precision control to two classical training-free components, allowing the VLA to focus on stage-specific skill dynamics. PGX decomposes long-horizon loco-manipulation into three layers: (i) a predicate-based state machine governs task progression, using physical predicates to gate phase transitions, trigger recovery, and coordinate navigation and waiting. Shared predicate semantics connect offline demonstration segmentation, online execution, and stage-wise evaluation; (ii) VLA skills operate within active manipulation phases, with flat or stage-trained models concentrating on task-relevant actions; and (iii) world-coordinate locking (WCL) maintains spatial consistency through base station keeping, object-relative positioning, and world-anchored contact targets. We demonstrate the effectiveness of PGX with extensive experiments conducted on three simulated tasks and one real-world task using a Unitree G1 humanoid robot for long-horizon loco-manipulation, showing improvements in stage progression and task success rates. Project page is available at: https://kl-research.github.io/pgx

items.title: Realized versus Population Reliability: Anytime-Valid Self-Consistency Certification under Correlated Reasoning
items.abstract: Self-consistency certification treats repeated sampling from a language model as sequential evidence accumulation and stops when an anytime-valid e-process crosses a threshold, guaranteeing finite-sample Type I error control by Ville's inequality. Prior constructions assume sampled rollouts are conditionally independent. We show this assumption fails in practice: reasoning streams are positively correlated through shared reasoning prefixes or across-prompt heterogeneity, changing not merely certificate efficiency but the hypothesis certified. Modeling dependence via a per-unit latent state (the random-effects / intraclass-correlation structure) induces exchangeable, equi-correlated increments with correlation $ρ$. Correlation splits the single null into a realized null about the drawn belief and a population null about average model behavior, which coincide only when $ρ=0$. We show: (i) the standard betting e-process remains anytime-valid for the realized null, not the population null; (ii) read as a population-null test, a suitable mixture has asymptotic crossing probability at least $π=P(μ(Z)>0)$, potentially exceeding nominal $ε$; (iii) the within-unit mean's effective sample size saturates at $1/ρ$, so extra within-unit rollouts cannot restore population validity; and (iv) a prompt-level e-process restores population validity, with optimal allocation at one rollout per prompt under a pure rollout budget. Simulations and Claude Haiku 4.5 rollouts confirm this regime dependence: on GSM8K ($\hatρ=0.435$, $\hatθ=+0.96$) the gap is dormant, whereas on AIME ($\hatρ=0.480$, $\hatθ=-0.15$) the single-unit rule crosses on 24% of prompts at nominal $ε=0.05$, while the prompt-level procedure declines (0.00). This correctness result identifies which reliability claim an anytime-valid certificate actually supports under dependence.

items.title: Probing the "Conscious" Mind: Selective Access and Global Workspace in Vision-Language Models
items.abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) integrate visual and textual information, but their outputs do not reveal internal concept representations. Global workspace theory (GWT) proposes that information is selected from parallel brain processes, integrated in a shared workspace, and made available to specialised processes. We introduce the Multimodal Concept Lens (MC-Lens), a multimodal Jacobian lens, to study these functions in VLM concept processing. Its vision encoder and language decoder lenses map intermediate states to a shared semantic space defined by the decoder's output vocabulary to compare concept accessibility across modalities. MC-Lens supports internal concept interventions to examine the role of accessed concepts in downstream computation. (i) Accessibility and selective access. Multimodal concept information is readable in intermediate states and selectively accessible as tasks require. We extend "readout carriers" from one name token to a token set to better capture and express concept information and support counterfactual experiments. (ii) Concepts in downstream computation. Counterfactual experiments show that accessed concept information participates in downstream computation and reasoning. (iii) Development of cross-modal alignment and selective access. We develop two J-space metrics tracking the development of cross-modal concept alignment more clearly than hidden state cosine in controlled VLM training. The experiment also shows that reliable selective access develops later than concept accessibility. (iv) Shared functions across models. Across VLM families and sizes, we find shared patterns of concept accessibility, query-dependent selectivity and cross-task intervention effects despite differences in internal organisation. These findings offer an experimental basis to study GWT in multimodal artificial systems and how it can guide cross-modal alignment improvements.

items.title: Verify the Verifier: Specification-Grounded LLM Cross-Checking for Bugs That Escape UVM Scoreboards
items.abstract: A passing UVM regression shows the design agrees with the reference model on what the scoreboard checks, not that it meets the specification. Bugs that pass every test yet violate the specification, termed scoreboard escapes, survive mature testbenches. We present Verify the Verifier, to our knowledge the first framework whose LLM-based Anomaly Cross-Checker examines a passing regression's traces against the specification. Of 564 bugs inserted into four OpenTitan IPs, 68 are candidate scoreboard escapes: non-equivalent, exercised by the tests, yet passing. The framework confirmed 41 as scoreboard escapes with assertions failing on the buggy design and proven on the original.

items.title: ProtoDiffusion: Token-per-Layer Generative Modeling of Multi-Layer Images
items.abstract: Graphic designs are ordered compositions of RGBA layers whose separation enables selection, movement, and reuse. Existing layered models represent each layer with a full-canvas or region-sized spatial latent grid, so representation size grows with the cumulative spatial extent of the layers. We present ProtoDiffusion, a latent-diffusion framework built on ProtoVAE, a multi-layer variational autoencoder that encodes a design into one shared spatial prototype and one candidate vector per layer. Each candidate conditions a shared decoder to reconstruct its corresponding RGBA layer. For $N$ layers, the representation contains $HW+N$ tokens before backbone-specific packing, compared with $NHW$ for full-grid-per-layer representations. ProtoDiffusion jointly denoises the prototype and a fixed set of candidate slots, conditioned on an image or text, with bounding boxes as optional layout guidance. The model leaves unneeded slots empty and determines the number of layers and, in absence of boxes, their layout, requiring neither as input. The same architecture supports both image-to-design and text-to-design. ProtoVAE achieves high-fidelity reconstruction from its compact shared latent representation, reaching 40.43 dB PSNR on layer crops. On the LayerD evaluation split, image-to-design achieves RGB L1 scores of 0.040 with bounding boxes and 0.057 without, with box-guided alpha soft IoU (0.850) comparable to the strongest fine-tuned baseline (0.871). On merged images, text-to-design reaches 66.41 FID versus 86.84 for FLUX.2 [klein], achieves a 0.860 text-accuracy score, and runs $19.1\times$ faster than the same-backbone generation-then-decomposition cascade.

items.title: GEOHunter: Mapping a Generative Engine Optimization Network in the Wild
items.abstract: Generative engines synthesize retrieved web pages into answers, recommendations, and rankings. Generative engine optimization (GEO) services sell visibility in these answers by publishing promotional articles on user-generated-content (UGC) platforms for paying clients. Such promotion raises concerns in medical and financial domains, where misleading advice can cause harm. To study the severity of this problem, we measure one such paid-content operation across three major Chinese UGC platforms, uncovering 1,985 accounts associated with the network comprising 466,357 inferred promotional placements. We find that the network promotes products across diverse categories through a growing pool of accounts, conducting coordinated campaigns spanning months across multiple platforms while evolving its listicle content over time. Across nine generative engines from both the US and China, we find that 4.5% to 20% of retrievable cited pages are attributable to the network, depending on how strictly attribution is drawn. On eight of these engines, its clients are named in 52% of answers, against 68% for category leaders. Our work demonstrates the effectiveness of UGC GEO placement at influencing generative engine outcomes, and reveals content-level defenses as insufficient against coordinated UGC placements, where account-level and platform-level signals are necessary for proper defense.

items.title: Multi-institutional grading of Barrett's esophagus dysplasia without stain normalization using a pathology foundation model and multiple instance learning
items.abstract: Barrett's esophagus dysplasia grading suffers substantial inter-observer variability, particularly for low-grade dysplasia, complicating clinical decision-making. We conducted a retrospective multi-institutional diagnostic accuracy study of a foundation model-based deep learning system for dysplasia grading, using 969 H\&E-stained whole slide images from four institutions. Patch-level classifiers trained on expert annotations identified diagnostically relevant regions, followed by attribute-aware multiple instance learning for slide-level classification as non-dysplastic Barrett's esophagus (NDBE), low-grade dysplasia, or high-grade dysplasia. On a held-out test set (n = 130), macro-averaged AUC was 0.96 (95\% CI 0.93--0.98). For binary dysplasia detection, sensitivity was 98\% (80/82) and specificity 81\% (39/48), with a negative likelihood ratio of 0.030 and quadratic-weighted \kap{} of 0.83 against expert consensus. No high-grade dysplasia case was misclassified as NDBE. Performance was consistent across institutions without stain normalization, indicating that stain-robust foundation-model representations may remove the site-specific preprocessing that has constrained prior systems to institution-specific deployment.

items.title: MM-SystemOneBias: Evaluating Bias in Multimodal Jev-Style System One Decision Models
items.abstract: When multimodal decision models determine actions, moderation outcomes, or quality judgments, their reliability depends on preserving semantic decisions across presentation changes, ignoring irrelevant additions, and distinguishing information consistent with task evidence from information that conflicts with it. Existing evaluations study decision-interface biases and multimodal model behavior in separate settings, leaving no common protocol to compare multimodal decision models with their backbones on practical tasks. We introduce \textbf{MM-SystemOneBias}, which evaluates 13 models on 5,323 original instances from nine public datasets and 11 task scenarios using six paired interventions: option order, option label, external judgment, image--text description, irrelevant information, and rating scale. Across seven matched decision-model--backbone pairs, decision models are more stable under option-label, irrelevant-information, and rating-scale changes in all seven pairs; six pairs also show lower option-order flip rates. They incur smaller accuracy losses under incorrect external judgments in all seven pairs and conflicting descriptions in six. In six pairs, they gain less accuracy from correct external judgments and show less favorable accuracy changes under consistent descriptions. Among pairs with unchanged semantic decisions, mean absolute changes in answer probabilities range from 4.56 to 11.55 percentage points, revealing input effects that accuracy alone misses.

items.title: Replication of Agentic Security Events: Audit and Investigation (ROGUE-AI)
items.abstract: Agents based on large language models (LLMs) can now delete files and send payments on behalf of their users. News media reports routinely describe failures of these agents (e.g., Replit's coding agent deleting a production database), but a report often only says what went wrong and rarely (in)validates the incident or finds its root cause. Incident catalogs collect these reports, and benchmarks record whether agents fail, but neither replicates an incident nor tests the cause its report might identify. In this paper, we present ROGUE-AI (Replication of Agentic Security Events: Audit and Investigation), a multi-agent framework that closes the above gap and rebuilds each reported incident offline together with a matched control that lacks only the blamed cause, and runs agents on both. Our results suggest that ROGUE-AI is able to reproduce the reported harm in 89% of its 108 attempted replications. Agents built on five current GPT, Claude, Gemini and DeepSeek models made the reported mistake in 18% to 33% of runs, against at most 1% without the blamed cause. Of the 72 incidents with real-world harm, 62 had no underlying attacker, and in these, agents did what their task asked for but missed an ordinary hazard, such as a database shared with the live site. Replications without an attacker caused more harm than replications of prompt injection for all five models. Defenses against prompt injection look for injected instructions, but these replications contain none. Further, a warning after each tool output that names the hazard and its consequence lowered harm for all five models, whereas a note of the same length that does not mention the hazard left most of the harm in place. Built from real incidents, the ROGUE-AI replications form a reusable audit framework that vendors can rerun before each new release.

items.title: The Geometry of Lies: Knowledge and Persona Directions for Detecting Deception in Large Language Models
items.abstract: Linear probes are the cheapest LLM lie detectors but often fail to transfer across kinds of lie. Label-free directions from honest and deceptive role-play are untested at 70B scale and on lies about knowledge, where a lie and an honest denial can be identical. We widen a published persona bank with roles that deny knowledge they have, plus honest counterparts. At each model's middle layer the resulting persona direction ranks lies across Liars' Bench better than single-dataset probes on three of its four models; it fails on Qwen, even when Qwen stays in role far more often. On Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct it beats directions from a random persona bank, but its gain over the published direction is within the range of random widenings. On lies about knowledge, persona directions mainly track a reply's wording: where lies and honest denials share their words, our three main contrasts stay inside the random-direction band on Llama and Qwen and reach only its edge on Gemma, though on Mistral one clears it. A knowledge direction contrasts questions the model can answer with ones nobody can, each followed by the same scripted denial. It separates lies from identical honest denials on two models and narrowly on a third, but not on the fourth; its other results partly depend on the benchmark's wording. On the Gender-Secret fine-tune it clears the band by a few hundredths on Llama and fails on Mistral. The sum of the two directions ranks lies better than a supervised probe at the same depth on all four models (on one, both near chance) but is level with the persona direction on Llama's average and behind that probe on held-out lies. More varied role-play questions do not help the persona direction on Liars' Bench.

items.title: AURA: AUdio-dRiven streaming Avatar
items.abstract: Current audio-driven video diffusion models can synthesize realistic talking-head videos but generally require dozens of diffusion denoising steps over multi-second video chunks, making them unsuitable for streaming applications such as voice assistants and virtual avatars, where low-latency and online causal generation are required properties. AURA generates video chunk by chunk with a rolling KV cache, requiring only the audio of the current chunk to start generating, rather than a multi-second audio look-ahead like bidirectional models. It comes in two sizes: AURA 1.3B streams 576p video in real time on a single GPU (20.7 fps for a 16 Hz playback rate), making it suited to interactive avatar applications, and AURA 5B streams 720p video at 9.7 fps. Our two-stage distillation pipeline first aligns the causal student with the teacher, by training it to match the teacher's trajectories with fewer diffusion steps and a chunk-wise sliding window causal attention mask, then applies Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) with backward simulation to close the remaining quality gap. On standard talking-head benchmarks, AURA 1.3B runs 23x faster than its own bidirectional teacher and reaches a quality comparable to TalkVerse at a lower resolution, and AURA 5B matches its TalkVerse teacher at 720p while running 17x faster. To support reproducibility and further research on streaming avatar generation, we release the weights of both models along with a dataset of 30K synthetic videos and their precomputed teacher trajectories.

items.title: LLM GerryMandering: Separating Interactions from Additive Effects in LLM Audits
items.abstract: Intersectional bias arises when a model treats people who hold several marginalised identities at once differently from what their separate identities would predict. Auditing such intersectional subgroups remains a challenge: their number grows quadratically, and there is no agreed baseline for what independent attributes would predict. Without such a baseline, many existing audits flag a subgroup when it exceeds each attribute alone, a condition that attributes acting independently already satisfy. We test this standard criterion on 150 synthetic datasets built with no interaction. With the shuffle null, it flags 66.1 false subgroups per dataset on average, and at least one in every dataset. When we plant interactions of known size into these datasets, a repaired null lets the criterion recover only 32% of them. We introduce ADDIS (Additive Intersectional Screen), which fits an additive model over all attributes, scores each subgroup by its Additive Residual Distance (ARD) from that model's prediction, and tests it against a Freedman-Lane null. On our synthetic benchmark, ADDIS flags 0.09 false subgroups per dataset and recovers 84% of the same planted interactions. We then build IndiPersona, 10,000 synthetic Indian personas with six identity attributes, and audit 13 open language models. The standard criterion flags 7.1% of the 738 tested subgroups on average; ADDIS flags 3.0%. Gender identity crossed with sexual orientation is the largest pairing in every model, and counterfactual personas confirm it and additionally reveal a caste x class interaction in all but one model that the observational test lacked the data to detect. Much of what audits report as intersectional bias can thus arise from independent single-attribute effects alone, yet a small core of interactions survives.

items.title: Cost-Aware Agentic Feature Optimization System for Fleet-Scale Ranking Models
items.abstract: Large Web platforms operate large fleets of ranking models, each selecting features from a shared pool of tens of thousands. We present an end-to-end agentic system that optimizes features across the fleet under resource constraints shared across models and those set per model, such as feature pipeline cost and serving throughput (QPS), respectively. In this system, LLM agents propose hypotheses, and deterministic tools execute experiments and verify them. For each model, an LLM generates and shortlists cross features from a combinatorial candidate space, and all features are then ranked by several importance methods. Feature blending mixes these rankings into a single selection, using Pareto fronts across tasks for multi-task models. An LLM Researcher agent then tunes the feature selection in 10--25 asynchronous trials under resource caps, and a trimming step keeps the pipeline cost within budget. Across production models, the system improves normalized entropy by 0.31% on average within each model's budget, and the trimming step cuts pipeline cost by 2.3% with no regression beyond measurement noise. The optimized models were launched, and in online A/B tests they improved a primary online metric by 0.20%.

items.title: Backtracking Agent Applications Security Incidents
items.abstract: Agent applications are increasingly deployed, yet agent-specific attacks pose real threats to them. Upon a security incident, organizations backtrack to identify the CEP (compromise entry point), remediate the damage, and prevent its recurrence. The main artifacts available for backtracking are trajectory logs, which record agent functionalities, and source code; app(lication)-specific function call logs are often fairly limited. However, trajectory logs are at the agent functionality abstraction layer, while the CEP candidates are function calls at the app code execution layer. Due to this semantic gap, the analyst needs to manually inspect the relevant code for each CEP candidate to infer its corresponding agent functionality. In this work, we present Origin, a backtracking tool for the analyst to submit a small number of queries to identify CEPs that existing tools cannot provide. Our approach poses two challenges: (1) define the intermediate abstraction that captures the mapping relationships between the two semantic layers; (2) determine the region-to-variable mapping for constructing the cross-layer graph defined in the intermediate abstraction. Each region is a specific group of agent functionalities. Origin addresses the challenges by (1) the cross-layer dependency graph (CLDG) that connects region-inferred functions at the semantic level to the variables in the low-level taint propagation subgraph, plus the associated query language, and (2) the region inference algorithm. Case studies on five popular agent applications across eight attack incidents show that an analyst using Origin correctly identifies all the CEPs.

items.title: GLiDE: A Fast, Calibrated Decision Model Distilled from Reasoning Teachers
items.abstract: Decision models enable fast, confidence-aware decisions by scoring candidate answers in a single forward pass, without generating text or intermediate reasoning. Yet reasoning can substantially improve decision quality, raising the question of whether its benefits can be retained without the cost of generating it. We investigate this question with \textbf{GLiDE}, a family of decision models spanning 0.4B to 27B parameters. Building on Qwen hybrid language models, GLiDE enables bidirectional interactions between the context, question, and candidate answers by removing causal masking from full-attention layers. To transfer reasoning capabilities into single-pass inference, we combine soft-target distillation from multiple teachers, including a reasoning model, with progressive post-training on diverse decision tasks. We further explore parameter-free recurrent depth to increase inference-time computation without generating tokens. Across five model sizes, GLiDE lies on the performance--parameter Pareto frontier of the Hugging Face \DI{}, with each model outperforming evaluated alternatives of equal or smaller size. \dmtwo{} (27B) achieves a hidden-set score of 71.52, with an expected calibration error of 2.0\% and a median latency of 92.9\,ms on a single GPU. Further checkpoint averaging and parameter-free recurrent depth yield GLiDE~27B, which reaches 73.37 with an expected calibration error of 2.1\%.

items.title: FLUID: Flexible, Evidence-Grounded Situated Task Guidance
items.abstract: Real-time task guidance is inherently flexible: when an agent guides a user through a task, multiple responses and timings can be appropriate, and sometimes the best action is to remain silent. Existing benchmarks often miss this flexibility by treating synthesized dialogues as fixed targets for what to say and when to say it. We introduce FLUID (Flexible, Evidence-Grounded Situated Task Guidance), a unified framework for modeling, evaluating, and enabling flexible interaction in multimodal task guidance. Using naturally occurring human-human guidance from WTaG and HoloAssist, FLUID grounds interventions in their supporting evidence, necessity, and timing flexibility, and uses this representation both to evaluate flexible guidance and to build a real-time agent for task guidance. Our agent achieves the strongest overall balance of response correctness, intervention precision, timely guidance, and response latency among evaluated systems, while still leaving room for improvement in avoiding speech overlap. Together, FLUID moves situated task guidance beyond rigid reference matching toward more natural and adaptive human-AI interaction. Project page: https://fluid-guidance.github.io.

items.title: A new algorithmic approach for finding flat minima: critically damped Polyak stepsizes
items.abstract: We present a new adaptive stepsize rule that biases gradient descent toward flatter minima in both theory and practice, and establish the first uniform-in-time guarantees for both sharpness and loss reduction for a broad class of locally quadratic objectives. Our critically damped Polyak (CDP) stepsizes multiply the classical Polyak rule by $4$ and a mild damping factor. The factor $4$ is critical in that it produces equioscillations around the manifold of minimizers $\mathcal{M}$ to leading order. Damping provably drives convergence to $\mathcal{M}$. CDP thus operates at the edge of stability by adapting its stepsizes to local curvature. Once the loss is small, its projected iterates follow gradient descent on $\log{λ_1(\nabla^2 \mathcal{L})}$ along $\mathcal{M}$ to leading order, paralleling the flatness bias of normalized gradient descent (Arora et al., 2022). Unlike normalized gradient descent, CDP step lengths shrink with the distance to $\mathcal{M}$, enabling convergence to an interpolating solution that locally minimizes sharpness at finite learning rate. We establish our theory for a broad class of non-negative losses with locally quadratic Morse-Bott structure near $\mathcal{M}$, capturing regular interpolation regimes in smooth overparameterized neural networks. Empirically, CDP stepsizes produce a flattening effect similar to that of Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM, Foret et al., 2021), reducing sharpness even in settings beyond our theory, including nonlinear teacher-student networks and fine-tuning of pre-trained LLMs.

items.title: Introducing ReTiNA-Cinema: Real-Time Neuro-Augmented Cinema via Generative AI
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is currently revolutionizing content creation across various media. Between those who fear it will replace human creativity and those who regard it solely as a tool, many in the creative industries are beginning to view generative AI as a collaborator. Yet interaction with these systems often relies on discrete, turn-based prompting that can interrupt flow and constrain expression to symbolic text. We explore physiological signals as a source of continuous adaptation without explicit commands, as a path toward embodied co-creation. This paper presents ReTiNA-Cinema, a methodological proof-of-concept that integrates electroencephalography (EEG) with generative AI to enable physiologically guided visual modulation of cinematic material. By linking physiological activity to the evolving appearance of a film, the system provides a basis for exploring embodied sense-making, in which viewers' bodily responses contribute to shaping the sensory experience through which they interpret the unfolding scenes. The system combines real-time EEG signal processing with a generative AI pipeline based on Stable Diffusion Turbo for frame-level image transformation. Single-user and two-user configurations map EEG-derived features to prompt selection and transformation strength. ReTiNA-Cinema offers a framework for exploring how the physiology of viewers might influence a film's visual presentation, extending the possibilities for participation in cinematic experiences and storytelling. This system raises questions about the effects on engagement, perceived agency, and emotional response, which remain open to future empirical study. Video illustrations: https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLMu36WzSQKiVeBnrUdwUAoUhqLqGX3_bw and implementation: https://github.com/KairosHive/retina-cinema.

items.title: Monte Carlo Pass Search for Setpieces
items.abstract: Set pieces produce about a third of non-penalty expected goals (xG), yet they are usually evaluated by what happened next. We present Monte Carlo Pass Search (MCPS) for set pieces, which treats a corner or a lofted free kick as a distribution over plausible executions and plausible futures instead of a single realised event. From the pre-kick state, MCPS proposes counterfactual deliveries and counterfactual set-ups (where the attackers stand at the kick), plays each out many times in a world model (3D ball physics, a generative model of all 22 players, the keeper's come-or-stay decision and a Player-to-Touch model) and scores every future with a value model. On 249 deliveries from 30 Serie A 2025/26 matches, with every model applied only to matches it never saw, the best available delivery is worth 0.0085 xG more than the one kicked (+28 %), mainly because it reaches an attacker before the keeper. Searching where the attackers stand as well adds +0.0027 xG with the observed ball and +0.0033 on top of the best ball; designing their runs too adds +0.0007 more. We show how to keep such a search honest, and estimate how much more data each component needs before a club could rely on it.
